A federal appeals court revived the Texas law in May, putting Arizona’s version back in play on July 14.
But Mayes rebutted that it’s too early to know what impact the state crime provision could have.
Instead, Mayes warned the court that blocking the law would amount to undermining the will of Arizonans who voted for it two years ago and tying the hands of law enforcement officials.

text:
Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes says it’s too soon for a lawsuit to be filed against a 2024 law that would allow local police officers to arrest unauthorized immigrants because no one has been arrested under it yet.

Earlier this month, the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, a legal nonprofit that offers pro bono defense for people facing deportation proceedings, filed a lawsuit against the law, arguing that it flies in the face of federal authority and should be permanently blocked. The group requested that the law be paused while litigation continues, but Mayes and Republican legislative leaders, who are all defending the 2024 law, argue that doing so would be the wrong move.

Two years ago, 61% of voters sided with Proposition 314, also called the “Secure the Border Act.” The ballot measure enshrined new criminal penalties into state law, including one that punishes people who use fraudulent documentation to apply for public benefits or employment and another that carries a prison sentence for those convicted of knowingly selling lethal fentanyl.

The most controversial provision, known in court filings as “Section 5,” makes it a state crime for someone to cross Arizona’s southern border without authorization anywhere but at an official port of entry. First time offenders face a class 1 misdemeanor, which means up to six months in jail.

The Republican lawmakers who wrote Prop. 314 anticipated a legal challenge, so they froze Section 5’s effective date until 60 days after a similar law in Texas, itself mired in litigation at the time, was implemented. A federal appeals court revived the Texas law in May, putting Arizona’s version back in play on July 14.

Mayes, who is mounting a defense of the law in court despite her vocal criticism while the ballot measure was being crafted, said too much is still unknown for the law to be challenged. The Democrat pointed out that the Florence Project doesn’t have any clients who have been charged under Section 5, putting the legal group’s ability to contest the law in doubt and rendering its arguments that the law will lead to unconstitutional arrests purely speculative.

“Because Section 5 has barely gone into effect, Florence Project has not shown and likely cannot show that anyone has been subject to arrest, detention, or prosecution for violating the illegal entry provision,” wrote Assistant Attorney General Timothy Horley.

To establish their legal standing in the case, the Florence Project warned the court that implementing the law could result in a wave of arrests across the state and force its attorneys to take on more cases or travel longer distances, jeopardizing the legal group’s ability to provide services to its clients and potentially resulting in missing critical hearings.

But Mayes rebutted that it’s too early to know what impact the state crime provision could have. She argued that arrests could just as likely be concentrated in the southern part of the state.

The law outlines a list of criteria for arrests. That list includes a law enforcement officer witnessing a suspected illegal border crossing, video footage of someone doing so or other “constitutionally sufficient indicia of probable cause,” which critics have said is too vague to prevent discriminatory arrests.

Mayes, however, was unconvinced by assertions from the Florence Project that anyone, even immigrants who’ve lived in the state for years or citizens could be targeted, saying that the law’s delayed deadline means its penalties only apply to people suspected of crossing the border on or after July 14. Mayes added that it’s also unclear how much of their resources law enforcement agencies will choose to devote to monitoring the southern border or looking for people who may be eligible for arrest under the law.

Instead, Mayes warned the court that blocking the law would amount to undermining the will of Arizonans who voted for it two years ago and tying the hands of law enforcement officials.

“There is a strong public interest in preventing dangerous cross-border crimes, like human trafficking and drug smuggling,” reads the brief. “Restraining Section 5 will take away from law enforcement authorities a method that the Legislature and the voters of Arizona have decided would make the state safer.”

description:
The states argue that the administration is improperly using federal grants to pressure them into assisting the federal government with civil immigration enforcement and into changing how they administer elections.
States that do not comply with the administration’s election requirements could lose at least 20% of their counterterrorism funding.
The administration also is seeking to require states to devote law enforcement resources to assisting federal immigration authorities, according to the lawsuit.
“FEMA cannot use counterterrorism and other essential federal funding as a weapon to coerce states into assisting with civil immigration enforcement or to change our election administration,” Davenport said.
It is the latest in a series of legal challenges brought by New Jersey and other states over the administration’s attempts to attach policy requirements to federal grants.
text:
Lawsuit says Trump administration is improperly tying emergency funding to immigration enforcement and election changes

New Jersey and 25 other states are suing the Trump administration over new conditions imposed on states in order to receive billions of dollars in federal counterterrorism and emergency-preparedness grants.

The lawsuit, filed by a coalition co-led by New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, challenges requirements imposed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for 2026 funding.

The states argue that the administration is improperly using federal grants to pressure them into assisting the federal government with civil immigration enforcement and into changing how they administer elections. The lawsuit also challenges a condition that the states say would allow federal officials to terminate grants at any time and for any reason.

New Jersey receives more than $55 million annually through the federal Homeland Security Grant Program. State and local governments use the money to prepare for and respond to terrorism, cyberattacks, and other threats.

States that do not comply with the administration’s election requirements could lose at least 20% of their counterterrorism funding.

The requirements include adopting paper ballots, manually auditing 5% of voting systems, using an undisclosed federal method to reconcile voters and ballots, and checking every registered voter and election worker through the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system.

The states contend that the citizenship database can incorrectly identify U.S. citizens as noncitizens and that election-related requirements have no connection to the counterterrorism funding authorized by Congress.

The administration also is seeking to require states to devote law enforcement resources to assisting federal immigration authorities, according to the lawsuit. A federal judge blocked similar conditions last year.

“FEMA cannot use counterterrorism and other essential federal funding as a weapon to coerce states into assisting with civil immigration enforcement or to change our election administration,” Davenport said.

The lawsuit alleges that the conditions violate federal administrative law and the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution. It is the latest in a series of legal challenges brought by New Jersey and other states over the administration’s attempts to attach policy requirements to federal grants.

text:
Where a petitioner who is detained in Plymouth County Correctional Facility has requested habeas corpus relief, his petition should be granted because he has successfully established a due process violation under Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 332 (1976).

“Petitioner alleges that his detention is unlawful because his detention is pursuant to 8 U.S.C. 1226(a), which requires a bond hearing, rather than 8 U.S.C. §1231(a), which requires mandatory detention. Under this theory, Petitioner’s detention allegedly violates both the Due Process Clause and the Administrative Procedure Act. Petitioner further alleges that his detention violates the Due Process Clause because Respondents are interfering with his right to the adjudication of his I-130 application. …

“Petitioner argues that Respondents violate his Due Process rights by interfering with his right to the adjudication of his I-130 application. …

“… Under the Mathews test, courts look to: (1) ‘the private interest that will be affected by the official action;’ (2) ‘the risk of an erroneous deprivation of such interest through the procedures used, and the probable value, if any, of additional or substitute procedural safeguards;’ and (3) ‘the Government’s interest, including the function involved and the fiscal and administrative burdens that the additional or substitute procedural requirement would entail.’ Mathews, 424 U.S. at 335. …

“Under Section 1154(a)(1)(A)(i), non-citizen spouses of United States citizens ‘may file a [I-130] petition with the Attorney General.’ 8 U.S.C. §1154(a)(1)(A)(i). This language provides non-citizens spouses of United States citizens with an unqualified right to file an I-130 application. The right to apply carries with it the right to have the I-130 adjudicated. … Accordingly, Petitioner has a due process-protected right to the adjudication of his I-130 Form. …

“The right to adjudication of an I-130 application includes the right ‘to be free from undue interference while undertaking the mandated process.’ … When a petitioner’s detention interferes with their right to adjudication, that detention is unlawful. …

“Petitioner submitted an I-130 application and argues that his detention interferes with his right to participate in the adjudication of that application. Specifically, the Government has requested Petitioner’s appearance at an interview, which petitioner cannot attend because he is currently detained. Respondents have not indicated a willingness to either waive the interview or make Petitioner available for the interview. … Accordingly, Petitioner’s detention interferes with his Due Process protected right to the adjudication of his I-130.

“This result does not change because the ultimate outcome of the I-130 adjudication is in the Government’s discretion. Petitioner is not seeking the grant of his I-130. Instead, he is seeking the adjudication of the application. …

“Having held that Petitioner has a protected interest in the right to the adjudication of his I-130, the Court turns to the Mathews balancing test. …

“In sum, the Mathews factors weigh definitively in favor of relief. …

“Having concluded that Petitioner has successfully established a due process violation, the Court next considers what relief he is due. In this area, courts have a fair degree of flexibility. …

“In cases where petitioners’ detention prevents them from seeking lawful status, courts have ordered immediate release from ICE custody. … Accordingly, the Court orders Respondents to immediately release Petitioner from ICE custody, subject to reasonable conditions of release.”

Ruiz Sencion v. Moniz, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-361-26) (11 pages) (Kelley, J.) (Civil Action No. 26-CV-12394-AK) (July 17, 2026).

text:
“So angry just witnessed Ice [sic] abduction of Ukrainian immigrant in SF international airport,” Robinson wrote in the Instagram post. “I have no words. This is unreal.”

Bystanders were able to document the woman’s name and contact information before she was cuffed to a wheelchair and led away by the agents, according to a follow-up post on Instagram by the hotline and advocacy group Stop ICE.

Doug Yakel, spokesperson for the San Francisco International Airport, told Gazetteer SF that SFO officials do not have any details on the incident beyond what was published on social media.

“ICE and DHS are federal agencies that operate outside the jurisdiction of US airports, including SFO. As a result, we are not involved in any decisions about their operations, nor are we notified when they occur,” Yakel said.

In a statement to Gazetteer, an unnamed DHS spokesperson confirmed the arrest happened on July 22 and alleged that Iryna Gorb, of Ukraine, entered the US in 2010 and overstayed her visa. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings, according to DHS.

Gazetteer has reached out to the mayor’s office and Robinson, and will update this story as we receive more information.

text:
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general are suing the Trump administration over imposing what they contend are “unlawful” conditions on federal grants intended to help states prepare and respond to disasters.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Rhode Island on Thursday, argues that the Department of Homeland Security and Federal Emergency Management Agency have been using their control over billions of dollars in federal grants to operate what the attorneys general see as an aggressive “campaign of coercion” to adopt the Trump administration’s preferred voting and immigration policies, according to the complaint.

“Congress never gave DHS or FEMA authority to rewrite state election law, require cooperation with federal immigration agents, or terminate federal funding streams at any time and for any reason,” the lawsuit stated. The legal action was filed by a coalition of 24 attorneys general and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, both Democrats.

A spokesperson for the White House did not respond to a request for comment.

At the crux of their legal complaint are two federal programs: the Homeland Security Grant Program, which was established by Congress as a response to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, and the Emergency Management Performance Grant Program, which helps states pay for emergency management staff who plan for and respond to natural disasters and mass casualty events, as well as software programs used by state emergency operations centers.

For the homeland security grant, the Trump administration has attached “radical” new terms based on Trump’s preferred policies, the states contend.

These terms include verifying the citizenship of all individuals in state voter databases, transitioning their voting systems to equipment that reads hand-marked paper ballots and conducting post-election audits “according to nonexistent guidelines to be set by the Secretary of Homeland Security,” according to the complaint.

And the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA have threatened to make states “promise to devote their scarce resources to the federal government’s own task of civil immigration enforcement” in order to receive both the homeland security and the emergency management grants, according to the complaint.

At a news conference Thursday, Bonta laid out the stakes.

“These grants help communities prepare for emergencies before disaster strikes,” he said. “They support emergency management personnel, strengthen disaster response capabilities, improve coordination among first responders, and help protect our residents when they need government the most.”

The Trump administration restrictions would mean “our communities would have fewer resources to prepare for wildfires, earthquakes, floods, terrorist threats, and other emergencies,” Bonta stated.

“Time after time, courts have told Trump’s corrupt administration that it can’t coerce California into doing its bidding by threatening to withhold public safety funding,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement. “Yet, they’re coming back for more. This time they’re demanding states rewrite their own election laws to access money that pays for public safety readiness and response, and that Congress already approved. We simply won’t allow it.”

title: This Seattle-area mechanic offers free tows for vehicles left behind after ICE arrests - KUOW
description:
Tepale said he’s seen a few cars left behind after ICE arrests earlier this year, but lately it’s far more.
The handful of cars he’s picked up are just a few of the dozens of others left behind.
They’ve been researching how ICE arrests happen, watching for immigrant rights violations, and warning of further human rights violations.
Tepale is no stranger to ICE, or being weary of them, or the politics that bring ICE agents into his neighborhood.
So far, Tepale’s successfully found people connected to most of the cars he’s towed, including the Suburban.
text:
Angel Tepale was halfway under an SUV he was hooking up to pull onto his flatbed tow truck. He searched for a good anchor point to pull the rest of the car onto the bed. The front wheels of the Suburban were already on the lowered truck bed. Tepale's black work books and pants were the only thing visible under the afternoon sun of a South King County sky.

“I wish I can change the law,” he said, “but that is just a wish because it ain't happening, and it's not gonna happen anytime soon.”

For the past few weeks Tepale has been picking up after ICE a lot throughout the county, towing away cars left behind after an arrest. He’s towed away at least 11 so far.

When ICE agents make a stop and a car is left behind they say they let the people they arrest make arrangements to pick up the vehicle, or call local dispatch to get it towed. In some cases it’s taken to an impound lot, then fees accumulate and it’s on the family to pay.

Sometimes Tepale will get the call. He takes the vehicles to a small lot near his Seattle area mechanic’s shop. But unlike other towing companies, Tepale offers his service for free.

Among the cars in the lot is a beat up gold Toyota Camry, an obvious commuter car, that has sat unclaimed for weeks after it was left by the side of the road after an ICE arrest.

“Working class people, going to work,” Tepale said in Spanish, “They [ICE] just come and pick you up, and they cover their faces, so you don't know if you've been picked up by ICE or being picked up [for] ransom.”

After he’s done pulling the Suburban SUV onto the bed of his truck he hops into the cabin of his flatbed truck. It’s a two-seater with a bench in the back, and a lot of cup holder space for clutter. There’s big open windows, and a pile of tools between the passenger seat, and the driver. On a warm day it smells like a mix of oxidized metals, a hint of sweet antifreeze, and years of elbow grease.

Tepale said he’s seen a few cars left behind after ICE arrests earlier this year, but lately it’s far more. The handful of cars he’s picked up are just a few of the dozens of others left behind. It’s part of a nationwide surge overshadowed by the World Cup.

Immigration attorneys said they have also seen a spike in new cases from the Seattle suburbs – a hotbed for immigration enforcement. Researchers at the University of Washington’s Center for Human Rights has confirmed 50 arrests that happened statewide in June — all connected to immigration officers searching license plate info in Washington state databases. But that number is likely an undercount.

Angelina Godoy, is the director of research at the Human Rights Center. They’ve been researching how ICE arrests happen, watching for immigrant rights violations, and warning of further human rights violations.

“They go physically to the site of a place which they define as a high target area or target- rich environment,” Godoy said, “which is kind of a euphemism really just for a place where they expect to find a lot of people of color, a lot of immigrants.”

ICE officials said they use information-based leads to identify and arrest people in what they call targeted enforcement. According to court testimony by ICE agents, during a spike in arrests in the Pacific Northwest in December — they would scan license plates at random to identify potential targets. Godoy said a lot of this takes place outside hardware stores or Latino groceries. Someone can be identified, and then later arrested within an hour and as quickly as 10 minutes. Sometimes warrants have been signed after an arrest was made.

“To call that targeted is only targeted in the sense of targeting an entire community or an entire neighborhood or an entire ethnicity,” Godoy said.

Sometimes ICE goes out to arrest one person but then picks up other people. This was the case in the fatal ICE shootings this month in Maine and Texas recently. In Washington, immigrant groups say a rise in arrests also is also illuminating ICE’s tendency for violence during what are largely non-criminal vehicle arrests.

“Reports include agents drawing their weapons on unarmed community members who are not resisting, smashing car windows, forcing people from their homes and vehicles, throwing people to the ground, and physically assaulting them,” wrote the Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network in a press release.

ICE is also reporting a rise in attacks nationwide. But, Department of Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin blames the immigrants in vehicles trying to evade arrest — and Democratic politicians that allegedly enable them and the residents, and citizens taking action to benefit immigrants in ICE encounters.

Tepale is no stranger to ICE, or being weary of them, or the politics that bring ICE agents into his neighborhood. For years he didn’t have legal status in the U.S. but that was a marriage, a citizenship ceremony, and eight years ago.

He’s seen arrests happen. A little while back a red truck was parked at a gas station near his shop. ICE smashed the guy’s windows and dragged him out. He’s frustrated about how immigrants are being violently arrested.

He also remembers the frustration he felt during the Obama administration, whose deportation numbers are a benchmark for the Trump administration’s own mass deportation goals.

”When I was trying to go through my paperwork, they would take my money, they would take my taxes from my business, they would take the taxes that I pay as a business owner, but they would not look at me and be like, ‘You know what? He deserves an opportunity to become a resident,’ or anything, They did not look at me like that,” Tepale said.

He also has his critiques of the Biden administration. Amid all this frustration, he's decided to do what he can.

“ By me picking up the car and storing it here for a little bit and making the video to let people know, ‘Hey, come pick up your car,’ I hope I'm doing a good thing. That's the only thing I know that I can do,” Tepale said.

In Tepale’s designated lot, the newly towed Suburban takes a spot near the beat-up gold Toyota Camry.

If the vehicles were there for any longer and Tepale was charging, the old owners might be better off buying a new one.

“You're not expecting that your loved one gets picked up,” Tepale said. “Now you have to pay extra money, which if you didn't have it… you just let it go and move on.”

For every ICE-related tow, Tepale makes a video and posts it to social media in hopes of getting the car back to the family.

His script varies, but there are two consistent lines that he repeats in his videos.

“Let's see if anyone recognizes this,” he said in Spanish. “If you do, send me a message.”

When he gets a response, he’ll cross reference personal info to make sure the cars go back to their rightful owners. But finding them isn’t always a sure thing. That’s not the only uncertainty.

Since he’s started his pro-bono work, ICE agents will occasionally drive by his shop.

“I don’t have fear, but I do feel that they’re going to do something to me. But then I tell myself, ‘I am not doing anything bad. I’m simply arriving after they’ve arrested them and all that,’” he said.

ICE agents have driven by and waved at Tepale and his coworkers. He takes it as them waving “goodbye.”

“They’ve tried to intimidate us,” he said.

So far, Tepale’s successfully found people connected to most of the cars he’s towed, including the Suburban. But there’s still the old Camry that’s been there for close to a month now.

Recently, he visited an address he suspected was connected to the Camry. When he got there to leave a note, the front door of the home was wide open.

But no one was home.

She brings two decades of international human rights work to this report.
Despite the obvious barrage of social media posts clearly showing concerning behavior by ICE agents, she explained to me that as a researcher, she started with the data first.
“We’ve never seen immigration agents act at this scale and with the severity of misconduct, as we’ve just documented.
What Naureen and Denise describe is a practical and very doable replacement agency: an immigration management agency oriented toward service rather than force.
text:
The ACLU just released Agents of Chaos and Cruelty, a data-driven civil rights review of how immigration enforcement was carried out across eight states in 2025. Naureen Shah, the ACLU’s Director of Policy and Government Affairs for Immigration, and Denise Bell, the consultant who led the research, reviewed more than 1,200 enforcement incidents in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland, and New Mexico, and found more than 400 cases that involved misconduct by agents. Their central finding is that the tragic killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis are not aberrations, but are part of a consistent pattern of rogue, paramilitary-like behavior that should concern all Americans.

I spoke with Denise and Naureen because I wanted to understand more about how they came to this work, how they conducted the research, and why the ACLU chose this moment to issue such bold recommendations for systemic change (more on that in a minute).

Any project that involves detailed review of so many cases requires a diligent methodology, careful attention to detail, and experience documenting human rights abuses—which is why Denise Bell was perfect for this work. She brings two decades of international human rights work to this report. After the Dayton Peace Accords ended the war in the Balkans, she joined a United Nations mission to help refugees and internally displaced people return home, work that grew out of a conviction she still holds, that when the state turns its power against people and they cross a border, they become, as she said, “the constituents of no one.”

She began her career at Amnesty International working on Darfur, then earned a law degree and served with the Department of Justice at the New York Immigration Court, where she saw from the inside how a system staffed with capable judges is still stacked against the people standing in front of them. She later returned to Amnesty International USA to lead its campaigning and then its research on refugee and migrant rights, and she has worked on access to protection and pushed back against state overreach globally, nationally, and domestically ever since.

Drawing on this experience, Denise described how the research project began. Despite the obvious barrage of social media posts clearly showing concerning behavior by ICE agents, she explained to me that as a researcher, she started with the data first.

“We did not seek out a pattern. We did not seek out civil rights violations. We just reviewed what was out there publicly, and the pattern emerged.”

Looking at the data and drawing on her years of national and international experience in civil and human rights violations, Denise knew the patterns of systemic violence when she saw them. Long before ICE showed up in Minneapolis, Denise was already fearing the worst. Looking back over her notes from the fall of 2025, she told me that she found scribbled on one page a frightening but ultimately correct premonition:

“They’re going to kill somebody.”

ICE did kill someone—lots of people, in fact: two U.S. citizens, 50 people in ICE detention since the start of the current Trump administration, and at least another 10 people in a frightening but predictable wave of violence from officers who show up masked and unmarked to terrorize communities of immigrants and citizens alike. Since ICE appears unable to pull its punches, the ACLU’s careful documentation doesn’t either. The report shows that the rise of this 'national deportation policing force'—which includes ICE but extends to a wide range of complicit federal, state, and local agencies—is much bigger than just immigration:: these abuses “reveal a blueprint for expanding authoritarian rule in the United States, with profound consequences for everyone in America.”

The report chooses its opening case not in Minnesota but in Florida, and Denise walked through why. Floridalma Sanchez-Gomez, an asylum seeker with work authorization, was driving home with her two brothers when a traffic stop turned into her being tased twice in her own front yard, her home broken into with a crowbar, multiple federal agencies and a helicopter arriving within minutes, a thirteen-year-old returning to a broken home, and a U.S. citizen neighbor arrested for observing under Florida’s HALO law. Denise’s point is that this happened on an ordinary residential street, and that ordinariness is the finding.

“There was a shift to transform the agency into one that could sweep in as many people as possible, and thus it transformed society for everybody, because no one was off-limits, and no place was off-limits.”

As a geographer who works with enforcement data, what held my attention is the sheer scale of unhinged enforcement, and Naureen named the distinction that makes the scale matter. Immigration is a civil matter, not a criminal one, but the report documents agents behaving as an unaccountable occupying force.

“We’ve never seen immigration agents act at this scale and with the severity of misconduct, as we’ve just documented. … They’re acting more like a paramilitary agency, an internal security force.”

Naureen located the reason this continues in a single word: impunity.

“Impunity is what we see all around the world in places where torture and killings and abuse happens. It happens again and again, because people know they will get away with it.”

The report documents 437 incidents of likely racial profiling, and Naureen anchored that number in a fifteen-year-old in Illinois who was chased three blocks and tackled while waiting for a school bus, then asked whether he was a U.S. citizen. She connected it to a piece of the pattern that reaches everyone who witnesses it. Agents mask their faces, drive unmarked cars, and wear clothing that identifies no agency, so a person often cannot tell an arrest from an abduction or know whom to hold responsible. The consequence is that watching becomes dangerous.

“If we’re watching what’s happening, and we’re horrified by what’s happening, and we pull out our phones to record what’s happening, now we are in the crosshairs of what we call the National Deportation Policing Force.”

That force is not only ICE. Naureen described more than 2,000 state and local law enforcement agencies now signed up through the 287(g) program to take and make calls for ICE, which is the mechanism I have mapped in my own work on local deputization. It is how a national pattern gets built out of local police departments, and it is why the report treats these incidents as connected rather than episodic.

The part of the conversation that will draw the most attention is the affirmative vision, because the ACLU has called for a level of systemic change it never has before. Naureen argued that the system is built around enforcement when it should be built around management, and that mere tinkering will not fix it. We need substantial transformation.

“We want to replace ICE. That’s what we’re calling for as the ACLU for the first time. We want to replace ICE with that management system that is oriented towards getting people on a path.”

I was eager to talk more about this, because calls to abolish ICE have circulated for years and have often left me wanting, since an immigration system still exists on the books no matter which agency runs it. It’s not enough to want to tear something down; we have to have a vision for what we want to build in its place. What Naureen and Denise describe is a practical and very doable replacement agency: an immigration management agency oriented toward service rather than force.

This conversation belongs alongside the others I have hosted this year with the people assembling this record. Human Rights Watch reconstructed the federal surge in Minneapolis and the rising death rate inside ICE detention. Heidi Altman of the National Immigration Law Center walked through the enforcement money Congress approved and what the availability of that money drives. Nayna Gupta and Aaron Reichlin-Melnick of the American Immigration Council laid out what an immigration system built for compliance would actually require, where compliance only means something if the system is one that people can comply with. Agents of Chaos and Cruelty ties them together, from the killings to the funding to a concrete demand to replace the agency at the center of it.

I’m deeply grateful to Denise and Naureen for spending an hour with me on this incredibly impactful report. Download the report and please actually read it so that you understand what the data says about how immigration enforcement is creating chaos across our country right now.

READ THE REPORT

Timestamp of key themes

05:35 — How Naureen came to immigration work

09:02 — How Denise came to it, from Balkans refugee missions and Amnesty to the immigration courts

12:45 — What the report documents and what motivated it

21:47 — How they chose eight states, and why the pattern is systemic

26:51 — The Florida case study and what “no one is off-limits” means

31:10 — The HALO law, recording enforcement, and the National Deportation Policing Force

35:59 — What use of force actually looked like, beyond firearms

45:19 — Replacing enforcement with management, and calling to replace ICE

51:05 — Abolish versus replace, and an immigration agency built for management

53:13 — What a transparent agency would report, and the data going dark

56:28 — Closing takeaways and how to take action

Five Things You Can Do Right Now

Read the report. Download Agents of Chaos and Cruelty, and if it helps you focus the way it helps me, print it. If you can scroll on socials for an hour, you can read this. Your brain will thank you. 🧠

Take action with the ACLU. Go to aclu.org/action. Naureen pointed to a discharge petition on the American Dream and Promise Act, which could open a path to citizenship for roughly 4.4 million people, and asked people to request a meeting with their members of Congress during the August recess.

Support your local rapid-response network. Denise credited community responders in states like Illinois, Colorado, and California for surfacing and verifying incidents that no outlet would otherwise report. These are the networks documenting enforcement where you live, so get involved if you can. And if you need data driven training and support, reach out to us at Relevant Research about a potential partnership.

Know your rights before you record. Recording enforcement is protected in many places, but laws like Florida’s HALO law may expose observers to arrest depending on the circumstances and the state you are in. Learn what applies where you are before you find yourself in that position. If you have tips and resources, share them with me in the comments below.

Leave a comment

Share the report and this conversation. The value of this work depends on people seeing it. Send it to someone who still thinks Minneapolis was just an isolated incident rather than a systemic problem that should concern all of us.

Help Keep These Conversations Going

Federal immigration agents say a truck that crashed into a Virginia townhome during an enforcement operation was occupied by people who fled as officers were trying to make an arrest.

The crash happened around 6:46 a.m. July 22 in the 900 block of Sherwood Court in Sterling.

In a statement on Thursday, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said officers were having a targeted enforcement operation to arrest what the agency described as a "criminal illegal alien."

READ ALSO | ICE agents on scene of federal operation near Potomac River in Montgomery County

According to ICE, officers tried to pull over a truck occupied by someone matching the description of the target. The driver and passenger allegedly hopped out without putting the truck in park, causing it to roll down a hill and crash into a nearby home.

No one was hurt.

ICE said the person it was trying to nab has a criminal history that includes DUI, drug possession, property damage, robbery, possession of stolen property, possession of burglary tools, fraud, shoplifting, and violating a court order.

The Loudoun County Sheriff's Office previously told 7News it was not notified about the federal operation in advance and was not involved.

SEE MORE | Illegal immigrant arrested after woman fights off attacker on Virginia trail

Deputies responded after getting reports of the crash and focused on the safety of residents.

Loudoun County Fire and Rescue also responded, and a fire marshal later determined the home was structurally safe.

ICE said resisting officers and evading arrest are felonies and federal crimes.

It is unknown whether anyone has been taken into custody.

text:
A coalition of states is suing the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Department of Homeland Security, accusing the Trump administration of withholding hundreds of millions of dollars in disaster-preparedness and homeland security grants to force states to adopt its policies on elections and immigration.

The complaint challenges new conditions imposed on the funding that would require states to verify voter citizenship through a federal database, move toward hand-marked paper ballots, conduct federally prescribed election audits and cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.

The lawsuit was filed by a group of 25 states and the District of Columbia.

They estimate that FEMA could withhold at least 20% of Homeland Security Grant Program awards — about $148 million from the plaintiff states — and potentially terminate entire awards for continued noncompliance, moving forward.

DHS funds typically offer emergency-management support — reimbursing for first responders, bomb squads, cybersecurity, disaster response and security at houses of worship.

The lawsuit alleges DHS is using the funds as leverage over policies that the states argue are largely unrelated to those programs as part of a pressure campaign.

The lawsuit also challenges language that would permit FEMA to cancel grants that no longer align with the administration's changing priorities or view of the "national interest." The states argue that such authority would make multiyear federal awards unreliable and give the executive branch a way to redirect spending approved by Congress.

Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha, who's co-leading the case, accused the Trump administration of "threatening to jeopardize public safety by unlawfully withholding billions in critical funding."

"Congress allocated these funds to the states for preparing for and responding to emergencies including counterterrorism and natural disasters, and the executive branch has no legal say in the matter," Neronha said in a statement announcing the suit. "Federal emergency funding cannot and will not be held hostage from states."

A FEMA spokesperson told CBS News: "This partisan pushback from New Jersey, California, Illinois, and Rhode Island is nothing new. We fully expected these left-wing politicians to oppose common-sense measures designed to protect election security and safeguard the integrity of American democracy."

"This year, states must take critical, common-sense steps to protect U.S. elections before receiving their full Homeland Security Grant Program awards," FEMA's statement continued. "These new requirements will preserve election integrity."

Along with Rhode Island, the suit was joined by attorneys general from Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, as well as the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.

The states contend the conditions imposed by FEMA and DHS violate the Administrative Procedure Act and the Constitution's Spending Clause.

Attorneys General from the states and Washington, D.C., are now asking a federal judge in Rhode Island to block the conditions, void them nationwide as applied to the plaintiffs and require the agencies to issue funding documents.

title: As time runs out on TPS for Haitians, leaders and advocates in Boston urge Congress to take action
description:
The legal status of Haitians in the country with TPS is set to lapse by next week after a Supreme Court decision in June allowed the Trump administration to terminate the program for Haitians and Syrians.
A bill to extend TPS status to Haitian immigrants by three years passed in the U.S. House in April.

text:
City leaders, state officials and immigration advocates rallied on Boston's City Hall Plaza to urge Congress to extend Temporary Protected Status for Haitians living in the U.S.

A bill to extend TPS status to Haitian immigrants by three years passed in the U.S. House in April. The Senate version, sponsored by Massachusetts U.S. Sen. Ed Markey, remains in the upper chamber after it was blocked from passage on Wednesday.

On City Hall Plaza, Clara Raymond, originally from Léogâne, Haiti, danced to Creole lyrics, which she said translate to “Don’t be scared, everything gonna be alright.”

Raymond works with Haitians through the Immigrant Family Services Institute.

“I was expecting more Haitians," she said after tallying her community members around her. "They’re scared. They’re afraid ICE might be here.”

Speaking to the demonstrators and supporters during the rally, Wu acknowledged the tumult that the Haitian community has gone through.

“Even as pained as we are, as exhausted and angry as we are, my heart is still filled with gratitude for this community who show up time and time again whenever the moment demands it,” she said. “ We cannot function as a society, as a community, as an economy, as a people, when the bonds of trust are ripped apart.”

Uncertainty has gripped the Haitian community here for months. Many have lost their jobs as employers anticipate workers losing their legal status, despite pleas from public officials to keep workers in the interim. Gov. Maura Healey has warned of dire economic consequences of losing these workers in healthcare, construction and other fields.

Driscoll echoed that message on Thursday, saying Haitians are valuable contributors to Massachusetts communities, working in long-term caregiving, childcare, construction and small businesses.

“They pay taxes, they volunteer, they worship alongside us, and they're helping build a stronger Massachusetts every single day,” she said. “ We stand with them, we will fight with them, and we will not stop until justice is done.”

Louijeune, whose parents were Haitian immigrants, described being in a legal clinic where members of the community came with worries and questions.

“ People who have been here for decades who are now at a point of fear because they don't know what tomorrow will hold,” she said. “They're asking me, ‘Will I have my job? What will happen to my children?’”

Louijeune said conditions in Haiti are unsafe for many people to return to due to gang violence and widespread hunger.

The TPS program was initiated by Congress in 1990 to allow eligible migrants to live and work in the U.S. if their home countries were afflicted by natural disasters or conflicts. Haitians have been eligible for the status since a devastating earthquake in 2010.

Thousands of TPS holders live and work in Massachusetts, and the largest group hails from Haiti. Massachusetts is home to roughly 19,000 Haitians with temporary legal status, according to researchers at Princeton University who based their count on U.S. Census data.

text:
The U.S. government directed over one hundred Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) employees to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to a U.S. House Committee report published on July 10, 2026. The assignments began in late summer 2025, with most staff drawn from FEMA’s human capital and security offices. Lawmakers say the reassignments hampered FEMA’s disaster relief capacity at a difficult moment for the agency, which had already lost significant staff to deferred resignations and early retirements the year before. Additionally, the report states FEMA management pressured disaster relief staff to volunteer for assignments supporting both ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

The timing drew scrutiny because the detailing coincided with a heavy disaster season, including deadly Texas flooding in July 2025, raising questions about whether the agency had the staffing it needed when it mattered most.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) barred disaster relief organizations from assisting or encouraging undocumented immigration in August 2025, and FEMA’s detailing of agents to ICE followed shortly after. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) has also been asked to examine the impact of these staffing shifts on FEMA’s core mission.

In 2025, DHS updated its terms and conditions, adding provisions that require states and other recipients to cooperate with enforcing federal immigration law.
“Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump administration,” said a FEMA spokesperson.
This year, states must take critical, common-sense steps to protect U.S. elections before receiving their full Homeland Security Grant Program awards.
text:
(CN) — Over two dozen states took on the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA Thursday, filing suit over new election and immigration requirements to receive grants from the federal government.

DHS and FEMA violated the Administrative Procedure Act and the spending clause in the U.S. Constitution, the states argued, by imposing new election- and immigration-related requirements to receive billions in anti-terrorism and emergency response funds. The agencies are attempting to leverage the funds to “coerce” states into adopting the Trump administration’s preferred policies, the states said in their suit.

Twenty-five states — including California, Colorado, Arizona and Washington — and the District of Columbia filed suit in Rhode Island, claiming the change in requirements was retaliation after FEMA and DHS were unsuccessful in cutting federal funding from states they felt opposed the administration’s immigration agenda in a prior legal case.

One of FEMA’s largest grant programs, the Homeland Security Grant Program, is now requiring states to verify the citizenship of their registered voters against the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, the plaintiffs said, leaving over $740 million in funding in limbo. The funds for the program are intended to assist states in fighting and responding to terrorism.

FEMA has also updated its terms to cut funding to states at any time if it deems they are not in compliance with “agency priorities.” For discretionary awards, it could cut funds for “convenience,” the plaintiffs claimed.

But Congress never gave the agencies the authority to rewrite state election law, require cooperation with federal immigration enforcement or cut off funding for any reason, the states said, nor can conditions outlining eligibility for the funds be vague and ambiguous. The agencies are also required by the Administrative Procedure Act to analyze the impact the changes would have on each program, they added.

In 2025, DHS updated its terms and conditions, adding provisions that require states and other recipients to cooperate with enforcing federal immigration law. FEMA has also cut the funding for specific grant recipients it considers to be “sanctuary jurisdictions,” the plaintiffs said, calling the change fickle and unconstitutional.

“Plaintiff states have received these grants year over year and rely on them to fund critical preparedness, mitigation and relief efforts,” the plaintiffs said. “DHS now insists that the states are not entitled to these funds unless they help enforce federal immigration law.”

Following President Donald Trump’s push for nationalized elections, FEMA has now also imposed election conditions on Homeland Security Grant Program recipients, requiring them to transition electronic voting systems to equipment that accepts hand-marked paper ballots, conduct manual audits postelection, conduct ballot reconciliation, confirm the citizenship of election workers and use the SAVE program to conduct citizenship verification.

States and grant recipients will have 20% of grant funds withheld until the agency confirms they have complied with the election changes, the states said, arguing the change violates the Constitution, which tasks states with election administration.

“Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump administration,” said a FEMA spokesperson. “Concerns over voting processes, data security and registration practices have made it clear that action is required. This year, states must take critical, common-sense steps to protect U.S. elections before receiving their full Homeland Security Grant Program awards. These new requirements will preserve election integrity.”

The new election requirements are unlawful, “arbitrary and capricious” and ignore investments states have already made in election infrastructure, the plaintiffs said, adding states cannot comply with vague election guidelines DHS has not yet adopted.

“The election conditions impose conditions unrelated to the federal funding they encumber, requiring states to comply with specific policies regarding voter eligibility and vote tabulation as a condition for obtaining millions of dollars in funding to prevent and respond to terrorist attacks,” the plaintiffs said in their suit.

Federal law does not require states to use the SAVE program to regulate their voter roll databases, and many states have privacy laws preventing their election officials from sharing voter roll information with third parties, including the federal government.

“President Trump has little support for both his mass deportation agenda and his baseless claims of election fraud, so instead, he’s trying to bully state and local governments into adopting his preferred policies in exchange for much-needed funding,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said. “The administration has already lost similar fights in court, and we expect this latest unlawful attempt to fail as well. Our communities deserve better than to have essential resources caught up in political games.”

DHS is now preventing states from publicizing the presence of federal immigration enforcement operations, the plaintiffs said, and is also requiring access to confirm the immigration status of detainees in correctional facilities and information about residents’ citizenship status.

FEMA has also imposed a new termination clause on all of its grants, the states said, allowing it to cancel a grant if it “no longer advances the national interest” or for the agency’s convenience. Existing law doesn’t allow FEMA to cancel grants when the agency’s priorities later change, the states said.

The states criticized the new termination conditions, saying they “operate as unlawful coercion by threatening the total loss of critical preparedness and disaster-relief funding to extract compliance defendants could not lawfully compel directly.”

The plaintiffs are asking the court to issue an injunction requiring FEMA and DHS to send out funding opportunity notices that don’t include the election, immigration and termination conditions.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security’s top lawyer publicly called out what he dubbed the “worst of the worst” judges who’ve ruled against the administration’s immigration agenda, escalating tensions between the judiciary and government officials.

James Percival, DHS’ general counsel, highlighted the four federal district judges by name in a series of posts on the social media platform X on Thursday, which he described as a new series titled “Worst of the Worst, District Judge Edition.” The series plays off the department’s practice of highlighting what it calls the “worst of the worst” immigrants deported.

Administration officials have frequently criticized the federal judges who’ve ruled against President Donald Trump’s priorities, even as threats to the federal judiciary rise.

Percival targeted two federal judges in Illinois and Massachusetts who ruled to temporarily preserve deportation protections for certain immigrants from Burma and Somalia while litigation continued, and blamed one for setting what he called a “deliberately sluggish” case schedule.

He also named the Maryland federal judge who oversaw litigation challenging the removal of Kilmar Abrego Garcia to a mega prison in El Salvador and a California federal judge handling litigation over DHS’ response to immigration protests.

Philip Pro, a retired Nevada federal judge, called the social media post “terribly disappointing” and “irresponsible” to see from a high-level government official and attorney. He also warned that by singling out judges posting on social media, the language could be amplified and drive threats to the judges.

“It erodes the public confidence in the judiciary, it weakens public faith in the law, and it’s amplified many times over when it’s done through social media,” said Pro, who is a member of Keep Our Republic’s Article III Coalition, a group of retired federal judges who advocate for judicial independence.

A DHS spokesperson said in a statement that Percival’s social media thread “is nothing more than a factual review of judicial decisions and their real-world consequences.”

“If accurately describing a judge’s rulings is controversial, the issue isn’t the reporting, it’s the rulings themselves. The record speaks for itself. Facts aren’t attacks,” the spokesperson said.

Percival is the latest senior official to publicly blast federal judges for adverse rulings.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a legal conference last year that there’s a “war” against the federal judiciary. Blanche later walked back those comments, saying in written responses to senators this month that the Justice Department “is not at war with the federal judiciary” and that his remarks “were not directed at judges.”

Trump also tore into Supreme Court justices who ruled against his signature tariffs, calling them “fools” and “lapdogs.” House Republicans have also filed impeachment resolutions against judges for ruling against the administration.

Top judiciary officials have called to tone down this rhetoric, as judges face rising threats. The US Marshals Service, which protects the judiciary, tracked 564 threats against federal judges last fiscal year, up from 509 the year prior.

Justice Elena Kagan, testifying before congressional spending panels earlier this month, said heated rhetoric toward judges and justices is “dangerous” to their security.

“When political figures of any stripe are trying to intimidate judges and justices to do things that they like, rather than the things that they don’t, that’s where we really have crossed a line,” she said.

Kagan also noted, during remarks Thursday at the Ninth Circuit’s conference, that federal district judges have fewer security resources than the justices, leaving them vulnerable to attacks. The justices have round-the-clock security details, whereas federal district judges generally don’t have security teams at their personal residences.

“We do right now have really excellent security arrangements in place. We’re trying to expand them, and improve them, but they are good. Whereas a typical district judge will not have that,” Kagan said. “Of course they can call on the Marshals Service. But you know, that can be even scarier.”

Percival, previously a top aide for Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) and Justice Department senior counsel, was confirmed as DHS general counsel by the Senate in December. Percival was questioned by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle during his confirmation hearing about the administration’s consideration of suspending habeas corpus to speed up deportations and, at one point, stumbled when he was asked to define the term.

He’s been outspoken in published opinion pieces in his role at DHS’ top attorney.

It asks a federal court to declare unlawful the new conditions, which demand changes in the way states administer elections, including by turning over their voter registration lists and the names of poll workers to the federal government.

“The Trump Administration is holding critical funding for homeland security and disaster response hostage in their latest attempt to take over our elections and perpetuate baseless conspiracy theories,” Shapiro said in a statement Thursday.

text:
A panel of federal judges on Thursday denied an injunction aiming to stop Tennessee’s redrawn congressional map — which splits majority-Black, majority-Democratic Memphis into three U.S. House districts — from going into effect before the August primary election.

The American Civil Liberties Union filed the lawsuit on behalf of voters, clergy and nonprofits in Memphis after Tennessee’s Republican-led legislature passed its new map in May. The lawsuit alleges lawmakers drew the map to dilute the votes of Black people, while lawmakers said they drew the map to give Republicans the advantage in all nine of Tennessee’s congressional districts.

The ACLU sought a preliminary injunction to halt use of the new map for the 2026 election cycle while the lawsuit continues to move through the court. Early voting for the August primary began on July 17.

A three-judge panel stated that the court presumes that lawmakers acted in good faith, and the lawsuit failed to show that “racial discrimination was a ‘substantial’ or ‘motivating’ factor behind the new map.” Without “direct evidence of racial motivation,” the plaintiffs “aren’t likely to succeed” on the merits of their case and therefore don’t meet the threshold for a preliminary injunction.

“The road to a reliably 9-0 map runs through Memphis,” the judges’ opinion states, “Thus, political motivations readily explain the map’s dilutive effects.”

While the court denied a preliminary injunction, the lawsuit itself remains pending.

Amber Sherman, a Memphis voter and one of the lawsuit’s plaintiffs, said in a statement that the court’s ruling continues to “further the disenfranchisement of Black voters in Memphis,” and she intends to continue fighting for equal representation.

“It’s painful to know we’ll head into another election under a map that was designed to weaken the voices of Black voters in Memphis,” Sherman stated. “We deserve the same opportunity to shape our future as anyone else.”

The three-judge panel includes Chief U.S. District Court Judge William Campbell Jr. (a Trump appointee), U.S. District Court Judge for the Western District of Kentucky Gregory Stivers (an Obama appointee) and 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals Judge John Nalbandian (a Trump appointee).

Campbell was assigned this case and two separate but similar federal lawsuits brought by the NAACP and League of Women Voters and by Democratic candidates and voters in districts affected by the new map.

Tennessee Democrats voluntarily dismissed their challenge in June shortly after Campbell denied their request for a temporary restraining order.

text:
The ACLU and National Immigration Law Center have renewed their challenge to a Tennessee law making illegal immigration a state crime after a federal judge dismissed a nearly identical lawsuit last month.

In their second lawsuit, filed July 17, the civil right groups are seeking an immediate and permanent halt to legislation that creates a misdemeanor crime for immigrants to remain in Tennessee more than 90 days after receiving a final removal order from an immigration judge.

Filed on behalf of two noncitizens who have lived for decades in Tennessee, the lawsuit is also seeking class action status in order to represent “hundreds if not thousands of noncitizens…subject to arrest, detention and prosecution,” under the new legislation, which took effect July 1.

The law was enacted as part of Tennessee Republicans’ so-called “Immigration 2026” agenda, which grew out of meetings between House Speaker Cameron Sexton and Stephen Miller, a White House advisor who is a key architect of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda. GOP lawmakers called the package of legislation targeting immigrants a “model for the nation.”

The legislation being challenged in court makes it a Class A criminal misdemeanor offense for noncitizens to intentionally remain in Tennessee more than 90 days after being issued a final deportation. Class A misdemeanors carry a sentence of up to one year in jail and a maximum $2,500 fine.

The legislation also makes it a crime for immigrants without legal status to enter, or attempt to enter, Tennessee, a provision that will not take effect unless the Supreme Court overturns a previous ruling out of Arizona that found states cannot usurp federal immigration law. The provision may also take effect if Congress acts to explicitly allow states to take on immigration enforcement duties.

The lawsuit contends Tennessee lawmakers violated the Constitution’s Supremacy clause, arguing the federal government alone can enforce immigration law

U.S. District Judge Eli Richardson last month dismissed the attorneys’ initial lawsuit, which made identical legal arguments, without ruling on its merits.

In his dismissal order, Richardson ruled two plaintiffs lacked standing to file suit, because they would not be subject to arrest under the new state law. Richardson called the case “more attorney-driven rather than client-driven.”

The same two plaintiffs, referred to only by first name in legal documents, are also plaintiffs in the refiled lawsuit. The second lawsuit provides greater detail about the individuals’ immigration status. The two plaintiffs are subject to arrest under the new Tennessee law, the lawsuit alleges.

text:
A July 21 emergency ruling by a federal court saved thousands of lawfully present immigrants from losing work authorization and asylum seekers from the automatic rejection of their cases.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services was scheduled to eliminate the benefits July 22 to satisfy parts of the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” passed by Republican majorities in Congress.

But they were spared when District Judge Nathaniel Gorton granted a motion temporarily blocking USCIS from terminating employment authorization for Temporary Protected Status holders and for some asylum seekers.

The Trump administration also was blocked from initiating removal proceedings against asylum seekers after closing their cases. “Here, the consequences faced by plaintiffs are potentially severe,” Gorton wrote.

The ruling stems from a lawsuit filed by the Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts, the National TPS Alliance, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, the Service Employees International Union and the 32BJ SEIU union.

The litigation argues the proposed USCIS policies illegally impose new barriers on TPS holders and asylum seekers, and that the government failed to provide due process and adequate notice of the changes.

Plaintiffs are represented by the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Network, Democracy Forward and the National Day Laborer Organizing Network.

“The Trump-Vance administration cannot use bureaucratic shortcuts to strip people of rights Congress guaranteed under our immigration laws,” said Democracy Forward President Skye Perryman. “The court’s ruling ensures thousands of families will not lose their livelihoods and their peace of mind while the courts consider the legality of these policies.”

Plaintiffs and legal co-counsel issued a statement explaining they are fighting to protect the legal process established by Congress.

“This decision protects thousands of asylum seekers and TPS holders from immediate and irreparable harm while this case moves forward. Without this relief, families who have followed the law and relied on longstanding humanitarian protections faced the sudden loss of their employment authorization and ability to support themselves through no fault of their own. Asylum seekers also faced rejection of their applications for relief. The order provides protections while the court considers the serious legal questions presented in this case.”

But Vanessa Cárdenas, executive director of America’s Voice, cautioned that the threats facing TPS holders and asylum seekers are not fully resolved.

“This ruling buys time, not safety. Enormous damage has already been done to employers and Americans who depend on the hard work of immigrant workers with legal status. Every person this policy targets is someone’s coworker, neighbor or caregiver, doing everything asked of them and still fearing for their livelihoods.”

And there will be no lasting solutions for immigrants as long as the Trump administration continues to widen its deportation campaign, she added. “Donald Trump and Stephen Miller are intent on continuing their relentless, violent and chaotic effort to delegalize immigrants so they can deport as many as possible. Congress must act now to protect TPS before the next ruling undoes today’s relief.”

​The following is a statement from ACE, the Association of American Universities, and the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities:

On Friday, February 7, 2025, the administration declared that it would cut funding for life-saving medical research. Its announcement that it would limit Facilities and Administrative (F&A) reimbursements to a 15% rate for all NIH research grants would have an immediate and dire impact on critical biomedical and health research nationwide. F&A costs are the real and necessary costs of conducting the groundbreaking research that has led to so many medical breakthroughs over the past decades. A cut to F&A for NIH grants is a cut to the medical research that helps countless American families whose loved ones face incurable diseases or untreatable debilitating conditions.

Besides harming the ability of research universities to continue doing critical NIH research that seeks out new and more effective approaches to treating cancer, heart disease, and dementia, among others, and translating basic science into cures, this cut would also undermine universities’ essential training of the next generation of biomedical and health science researchers. The loss of this American workforce pipeline would be a blow to the U.S. economy, to American science and innovation, to patients and their families, and to our nation’s position in the world as a leader in medical research.

It would be, quite simply, a self-inflicted wound.
