title: How "Mega Master" Immigration Hearings Are Changing Due Process in 2026
authors: Airington Law, explaining each step, you’ll find support
description:
Mega master immigration hearings are reshaping immigration court in 2026.
What Are Mega Master Immigration Hearings?
Mega master immigration hearings are large group preliminary hearings in removal proceedings.
In Minnesota, MinnPost reported that Fort Snelling joined the nationwide trend of holding “mega master” immigration hearings, raising due process concerns.
Why the Government Is Pushing Mass Hearings Now The government’s stated reason for accelerated immigration hearings is efficiency.
text:
The Daily Record’s San Antonio report described a docket where less than two dozen of 143 people appeared, and noted that many people who miss their initial appearance may be ordered deported if the judge finds they received proper notice.

Mega master immigration hearings are reshaping immigration court in 2026. For many immigrants, especially Latino families, the change affects whether they understand charges, find counsel, request more time, or fight removal.

Unlike traditional hearings, these mass dockets may include 100 or more people at once. Officials cite backlog concerns, while advocates warn that speed can weaken due process protections.

What Are Mega Master Immigration Hearings?

Mega master immigration hearings are large group preliminary hearings in removal proceedings. They are a high-volume version of the master calendar hearing, the first stage where the immigration court addresses basic issues such as pleadings, scheduling, representation, and possible forms of relief.

The difference is scale. Instead of a courtroom with a few dozen respondents, a mega master docket may place dozens or even more than 100 people before one immigration judge. The National Immigrant Justice Center has described these mass preliminary hearings as a process where many people, often without lawyers, appear together before a single judge and may feel pressured to move their cases forward quickly.

For an immigrant respondent, the difference can be serious. The judge may have less time to confirm whether you need an interpreter, explain rights clearly, or make sure each person understands the consequences of admitting allegations. In a crowded courtroom, it can also be harder to ask questions.

How Traditional Master Calendar Hearings Work

A traditional master calendar hearing is usually not a full trial. It is more like a procedural check-in. The immigration judge confirms identity and address, reviews the charging document, asks whether the person admits or denies the government’s allegations, and sets future deadlines.

Traditional master calendar hearings have always included multiple people on the same calendar. What is different now, according to the National Immigrant Justice Center’s explanation of mass hearings, is the volume, the use of written pleadings, and the lack of individualized assessment.

That is why advocates describe these proceedings as mass immigration hearings rather than ordinary scheduling events.

Where Are Mega Master Hearings Happening?

Mega master deportation hearings are no longer limited to one city. Reports in 2026 have identified mass docket practices or planned mega master settings in immigration courts including Virginia, Chicago, Boston, New York, San Antonio, Fort Snelling, New Orleans, and Indianapolis.

The scale varies by court. In San Antonio, The Daily Record reported that one immigration judge had 143 cases scheduled in a single day. That same report described the hearings as part of a broader effort to move cases faster through a system facing a multimillion-case backlog.

In Minnesota, MinnPost reported that Fort Snelling joined the nationwide trend of holding “mega master” immigration hearings, raising due process concerns.

For immigrants in Virginia, these changes matter even if their own hearing has not yet been converted into a mega master docket. Courts can reschedule hearings, advance dates, or issue updated notices. A person who moved, missed mail, or did not know how to check the court system may not realize a hearing date changed until the consequences are already severe.

Why the Government Is Pushing Mass Hearings Now

The government’s stated reason for accelerated immigration hearings is efficiency. Immigration courts have faced a severe backlog for years, and the current administration has made faster deportations a central policy goal. NPR connected the rise of mega master dockets to the effort to speed up deportation cases and move more people through immigration court at once.

The Department of Justice has also expanded the immigration judge corps. In May 2026, the DOJ announced that EOIR had sworn in 77 immigration judges and 5 temporary immigration judges, calling it the largest class of new adjudicators in EOIR’s history.

The announcement also stated that EOIR had hired 153 permanent immigration judges during the fiscal year and reduced the pending caseload from approximately 4 million to under 3.53 million.

More judges may help reduce delay. But bulk removal proceedings raise a separate question: whether processing more cases in less time can still protect fairness. A system can be faster and still fail if people do not receive meaningful notice, interpretation, access to counsel, or a real chance to explain their case.

Due Process Concerns Raised by Legal Advocates

Due process in immigration court generally means notice of the charges, a fair opportunity to respond, interpretation when needed, and a meaningful chance to present evidence. Removal proceedings are civil, not criminal, but the consequences can be life-changing: separation from children, return to danger, loss of employment, or removal from a long-established community.

Legal advocates have raised several concerns about mass deportation proceedings. Many respondents do not have lawyers. Without counsel, a person may not understand the difference between admitting a factual allegation and contesting removability. The courtroom environment may also pressure people to move quickly, while the judge may not have enough time to identify language barriers, trauma, fear of return, or possible eligibility for relief.

The National Immigrant Justice Center warned that mass hearings create room for error and due process violations, including the risk that people may unintentionally waive their rights to fight deportation. The American Immigration Lawyers Association has also raised concerns in reporting that large daily dockets may encourage speed over careful, case-by-case review, as reflected in coverage of the San Antonio mass hearings.

The Pleading Declaration Form Problem

One specific concern is the use of a pleading declaration form. This document may ask the respondent to admit or deny the Government’s allegations and to indicate how they want their case to proceed. For a lawyer, these terms have a technical meaning. For someone without legal representation, particularly someone reading in a second language, the form may be confusing.

The National Immigrant Justice Center reported that some judges instructed individuals to complete and file a “Respondent’s Pleading Declaration” form by a certain date. NIJC warned that completing the form could significantly shorten the court process and potentially speed up deportation.

If a person signs or submits a pleading form without understanding it, the court may treat key issues as admitted. That can make the case move faster toward removal and may limit later arguments. In an immigration court mass docket, where time is limited and many people are waiting, the risk of confusion grows.

What Happens If You Miss a Rescheduled Hearing

Missing an immigration court hearing can lead to an in absentia removal order. That means the judge orders removal because the person did not appear. In mass hearing settings, this risk may increase if court dates are moved up, notices do not arrive, or the respondent does not know the hearing was rescheduled.

The Daily Record’s San Antonio report described a docket where less than two dozen of 143 people appeared, and noted that many people who miss their initial appearance may be ordered deported if the judge finds they received proper notice. NPR also reported that mega master hearings may result in more removal orders when people are not present or do not respond in court.

This is why hearing notices, address updates, and court checks matter. Anyone facing removal in Virginia should keep copies of every notice and understand when to seek help from deportation defense attorneys in Richmond if a court date has been moved, missed, or misunderstood. A missed hearing can change the entire posture of a case.

Legal Options for Immigrants Facing Removal Proceedings

People in removal proceedings may still have legal options, depending on their history, family ties, criminal record, fear of return, prior filings, and case stage. Possible relief may include asylum, withholding of removal, Convention Against Torture protection, cancellation, adjustment, waivers, voluntary departure, or humanitarian options, though deadlines are strict.

For Latino families, the hardest part is often knowing whether a case is truly hopeless or whether a legal defense still exists. That is where understanding your legal options before a final order becomes important. In a mega master setting, respondents may feel as though the outcome has already been decided. But the central question is whether a valid defense or form of relief must be preserved before deadlines pass.

The National Immigrant Justice Center has emphasized that immigrants should know their rights and seek qualified legal assistance so they are not rushed toward the irreversible harm of deportation.

How to Protect Your Rights in Immigration Court

The first step is to know the status of your case. EOIR maintains an Automated Case Information System that allows people to check certain court information online. The official court notice is still critical, but checking the system can help you confirm dates, times, and case status.

Then address updates are critical. Updating ICE or USCIS may not update the immigration court, and missed notices can lead to serious consequences. Do not sign or submit pleadings unless you understand them.

Ask for an interpreter, request time to find counsel, and state any fear of return. Mega master immigration hearings show why fairness, deadlines, and legal options matter before a fast hearing becomes a final order in court.

text:
San Diego Comic-Con is known for elaborate costumes, celebrity cameos and wild live-action stunts. But attendees of the world’s largest pop culture convention Thursday afternoon may still be surprised by the event awaiting them outside: An anti-ICE rally pegged to a Jewish day of mourning.

Progressive Jewish groups across the country this week are using the fast day of Tisha B’av to protest national immigration policies, gathering outside ICE facilities, immigration courts,city halls and in San Diego’s case, culminating at a convention center. Tisha B’av protests are also planned in Los Angeles, Maryland, Massachusetts and Washington, D.C.

Tisha B’av commemorates several Jewish national tragedies, including the destruction of the Holy Temple in Jerusalem nearly 2,000 years ago. Protest organizers connect the torment tied to the destruction and ensuing exile, recounted in the book of Lamentations, to the pain experienced by immigrant families today.

“We had our sacred spaces taken away from us and we became wanderers,” Rabbi Mike Rothbaum, leader of San Diego synagogue Dor Hadash and one of the protest organizers, said in an interview. “And what is happening to the people who are in our streets? They’ve already been made wanderers once — having to escape torture, persecution, degradation — and now we’re doing it to them again.”

The protesters in San Diego — representing Jewish groups, labor unions, left-wing political organizations and social justice nonprofits — will begin by reading from Lamentations outside the Edward J. Schwartz Federal Courthouse, where immigrants are often detained following their hearings. They then will march to the San Diego Convention Center. They also plan to recite kaddish for people who have died in ICE custody or at ICE protests.

The immigration protests are part of a long history of Jewish groups using Tisha B’av as an opportunity to reflect on social ills. And while they will occur across the country, the protests are not nationally organized, according to their organizers. Instead, each one has a particular local resonance.

“San Diego is a border city,” Rothbaum said, “and the fact that we have a government that says the people born on this side of the border are more important, more precious, more sacred than people born on the other side of that border is blasphemy.”

Rothbaum’s involvement in Tisha B’av immigration actions dates back to the first Trump administration, when he was working in Massachusetts. A similar rally will unfold there this week outside New England’s ICE headquarters.

That event will include an Erev Tisha B’av program led by the state’s Religious Action Center of Reform Judaism and the Jewish Alliance for Law and Social Action.

Cindy Rowe, the alliance’s president and CEO, will also speak about Tisha B’av at a rally at Boston City Hall to protect the temporary protected status of Haitian immigrants, which expires Thursday. Massachusetts is home to roughly 45,000 Haitian immigrants whose legal status could be in jeopardy after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled last month that President Trump has broad authority to deport them.

The expiration of Haitians’ temporary protected status on Tisha B’av was “a cruel twist of fate,” Rowe said.

Tisha B’av represents “a day of mourning for the destruction of communities, and that’s exactly what we’re seeing right now in our modern day,” Rowe said. “The destruction of our own community right in front of our eyes.”

More than a dozen Jewish groups — including several synagogues, a JCC and various social justice groups — are partnering with multifaith organizations and labor unions on a Thursday afternoon event in Los Angeles, which will include testimony from clergy who have witnessed the conditions of detention in ICE facilities.

These groups held a similar event last year, when the spectacle of immigration enforcement raids was winning daily headlines. The media focus has since dwindled, but ICE detentions continue apace, according to Brooke Wirtschafter, executive director of Jewish Partnership for Los Angeles, a progressive group that focuses on local issues like housing and immigration.

“It is very much alive and real in Los Angeles in 2026,” Wirtschafter said. “If it is less dramatic than it was in 2025, it’s still very active, and so it’s important to us to continue to raise the issue.”

Likewise, a Jewish-themed immigration protest outside Comic-Con might feel dissonant to the traveling fans encountering it. Rothbaum wants it to turn heads.

“I hope when they come out and they see this group — and then they see Jews are part of this group — that they’ll think for a second before they go to the next thing, ‘Hey, what is my ethical obligation?’” Rothbaum said. “What are Americans’ ethical obligations to the people who come here, either escaping torment or looking for a better life?”

description:

text:
Following the fatal shooting of a 25-year-old Colombian man by a federal agent, the issue of immigration enforcement has become a flashpoint in Maine's Senate race -- one of the most consequential of the year in the fight for control of the Senate.

On July 13, an ICE agent fatally shot Johan Sebastián Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, after agents tried to stop the car he was driving.

Guerrero was not the target of the operation, Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, told ABC News. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said that Guerrero "illegally entered the United States on September 1, 2023, via the southern border." The DHS spokesperson said Guerrero was granted a work permit in May 2025.

Following the shooting, hundreds of protestors gathered across Biddeford to express their criticism of ICE and support for the victim’s family.

Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary for Senate in June but withdrew just weeks later after a sexual assault allegation, which he denied, spent his campaign going after Republican Sen. Susan Collins for passing legislation that funded DHS. Platner formally ended his candidacy with a letter in which he slammed ICE in the final line.

Now it's former Maine Senate President and logger Troy Jackson who is poised to take on Collins once the party officially nominates him to replace Platner on the ballot this weekend.

Jackson, who has earned the endorsement of many progressives, has called ICE "a rogue agency," and said it "needs to be dismantled because they give us nothing in this country but heartache and racism."

DHS has condemned rhetoric against ICE, which they say is fueling vehicle attacks against federal officers.

The July 13 shooting also put a spotlight on Collins, who said after the shooting she urged DHS to "cease all non-urgent vehicle stops" and the administration temporarily did. However, soon after, President Donald Trump reversed the pause.

Collins, the Republican chair of the influential Senate Appropriations Committee, has portrayed herself as someone who has a direct line to the administration despite representing a blue state. In January, amid the federal government's deportation crackdown, Collins argued it was her conversations with former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem that led to a slowdown in operations -- which her opponent at the time refuted.

Lance Dutson, a Republican consultant who worked on Collins's previous reelection campaigns, told ABC News that while Democrats may point to Trump's reversal as proof that her relationship with the administration is ineffective, he doesn't believe it undercuts Collins. Instead, he said, it shows she's "doing her best" to leverage her position for the good of her constituents.

"The thing that Collins has done, regardless of who the president is, is that she's prioritized having a good relationship with the federal government in order to support Maine ... we're highly dependent on federal money to keep the state working," Dutson said.

Jackson, meanwhile, has gathered widespread support among labor unions, which may strengthen his message on the issue of immigration enforcement, said Rob Glover, a political science professor at the University of Maine.

"Labor unions is where he's consistently drawn his base of support. ... There are whole industries in Maine that really rely upon immigrant labor and people who are here on visas, and it's just really been a scary time for a lot of these communities," Glover said.

Glover added a clear challenge facing Jackson is whether he can build the same momentum that took Platner months to generate. The Platner campaign had raised over $21 million since the start of his bid before he dropped out of the race.

"Democrats in the state of Maine are going to fall in line behind Troy Jackson. ... The question is whether he can build," Glover said. "What was so amazing about Platner is he built this fundraising capacity that we've just never seen, and the ways in which people were so excited to be involved in his campaign, he had 15,000 active volunteers."

'Devastation, heartbreak, significant anger'

On the ground, progressive organizers describe a community reeling from both the shooting and the turmoil in the Senate race.

Rev. Jodi Cohen Hayashida, with the Maine People's Alliance, a progressive organizing group which endorsed Platner before he withdrew, said the two events have compounded one another.

"What I have been hearing is a combination of absolute devastation, heartbreak, significant anger," Hayashida said, adding that organizers had warned since a surge in ICE activity last winter that the agency's practices "were going to result in someone being killed."

"The Democratic establishment has failed the people of this state and of this country," Hayashida said, who also argued calling for the abolition of ICE is the "baseline" for candidates seeking to replace Platner.

Maine State Rep. Mana Abdi said the Democratic Party risks losing a generation of voters, including those energized by Platner's campaign, if the party doesn't take a strong enough position on immigration enforcement.

Despite that, Abdi said organizers are urging voters discouraged by the shooting and the Senate race not to disengage entirely.

"It's okay to feel disengaged," Abdi said. "Take the time you need, but come back."

text:
A proposal for the West Manchester Township Police to partner with ICE was withdrawn after public opposition.

The proposal is now back on the agenda for an upcoming township board meeting.

The 287(g) program allows local police to perform federal immigration enforcement duties.

West Manchester Township Police Chief John Snyder stood before an audience of residents and settled a controversy by telling them he would pull a proposal for his department to partner with ICE.

“I’ll make it easy for everybody. I’m going to withdraw it,” he said during the West Manchester Township board of supervisors March 26 meeting.

Snyder and the board had just listened to an hour-and-a-half of public comments on the proposal. All but two of the approximately 20 people who spoke voiced opposition to West Manchester partnering with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement through its federal 287(g) program.

Most of those who spoke identified themselves with West Manchester addresses or came from neighboring townships.

At the end of it, Snyder stood and acknowledged the opposition.

“The last thing I wanted to do was create any division. I tried to do what I believe was the right thing to bring this opportunity forward,” he said.

The crowd applauded the move.

Meanwhile, the township’s board had to figure out what to do next.

One idea was to table the proposal indefinitely. The crowd didn’t like that.

Another idea was to remove the proposal from the agenda since Snyder decided to withdraw it.

The board opted for the former suggestion and voted 2-1 to table the proposal amid a caveat by the township solicitor that the members were free to reconsider their decisions.

That was four months ago.

West Manchester Township puts ICE agreement back on the agenda

The township is now set to resurrect the matter.

The board’s agenda for the July 23 meeting includes a point to “approve, revise, table or deny entering into” the 287(g) agreement with ICE that was tabled in March.

Chief Snyder would only say two words to the York Daily Record for why he’s renewing the proposal: “public safety.”

>> Please consider subscribing to support local journalism.

Ron Ruman, one of the township’s three members, said he received an email about a week ago that the police department wanted to renew the proposal. He had opposed it in March, and he told the Daily Record that his sentiment hasn’t changed.

“I believe it will not be a good situation for the township,” Ruman said.

He believed the decision to table the measure meant the book would stay closed on it indefinitely.

“I thought we had dealt with it and was not expecting it to be brought up again,” he said.

Board Chairman Steve Harlacher disagreed, saying the board doesn’t have an action to “table indefinitely.”

“Every action involves a motion to ‘approve,’ ‘revise,’ ‘table’ or ‘deny,’” he said in an email. “I thought it was appropriate to ‘table’ the motion and it was (seconded) by Vice Chairman Ruman.”

The third board member, Felicia Dell, didn’t immediately respond to messages seeking comment. Dell is on the board as the successor to George Margetas, who won a special election in May to take a Pennsylvania House seat.

Should the board decide to approve the proposal, West Manchester would join Carroll Township, Hellam Township, West York Borough, Northern York County Regional and York County Regional as local police agencies that have entered into the 287(g) program.

They’re among the nearly 114 law enforcement agencies across Pennsylvania that have signed onto it since March 2025. ICE’s website shows the federal agency has 2,179 agreements with law enforcement in 39 states and two territories.

What is the 287(g) program?

The 287(g) program serves as a tool that President Donald Trump’s administration has used to help carry out his priority for aggressive immigration enforcement by broadening the federal government’s reach with police partnerships.

The program gets its name from a section and subsection added to the U.S. Immigration and Nationality Act in 1996, now as federal immigration law as part of Title 8 of the U.S. Code.

Those sections authorize the government to enter into agreements with law enforcement agencies as a way to effectively deputize officers to perform federal immigration enforcement duties under ICE supervision.

>>Want to stay up to date on the latest news? Sign up for our newsletters.

Snyder argued at the March meeting that the West Manchester department wouldn’t change or give up its autonomy to ICE under the agreement, and he assured the audience that officers wouldn't become drastic enforcers by "kicking doors in" or going into schools.

“The ICE people do not have operational control of West Manchester Township policemen,” he said then. “This is not going to change anything or any way we operate here in West Manchester.”

He argued the proposed partnership was about public safety, enforcing warrants and immigration detainers.

Margetas, while still serving as a township board member in March, added that West Manchester wouldn’t work for ICE under the partnership. He argued the agreement would give local police another tool to work with.

Ruman spoke against the proposal at the March meeting.

“Enforcing federal immigration law is not the job of our local police,” he argued.

His stance remains the same today.

“From my perspective, nothing has changed. The situation hasn’t changed,” he told the Daily Record.

He and Harlacher noted, which the township solicitor also brought up in March, that any item can return to the board at any time. Ruman pointed out that even if the board had voted to the deny the 287(g) agreement, the proposal still could have been brought back later.

How to attend or watch West Manchester Township board meeting

The West Manchester Township board meeting is scheduled to be held July 23 at the Township Municipal Building, 380 East Berlin Road, beginning at 7 p.m.

The meeting will also be streamed on the township’s YouTube channel.

text:
A Trump-appointed judge dealt the Trump administration a major setback Monday, tossing out its lawsuit against Minnesota's sanctuary immigration policies and ruling the state cannot be compelled to assist federal immigration enforcement.

The battle centered on whether the Trump administration can use the Supremacy Clause to knock down Minnesota's sanctuary laws, which include policies that bar local officials from holding immigrants solely on ICE detainers, restrict participation in federal immigration enforcement and limit the sharing of driver's license and immigration-related data with ICE.

The Justice Department argued Minnesota's restrictions illegally hinder ICE, but Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud rejected that argument, ruling states have the constitutional authority to decide how their own officials participate in immigration enforcement.

In a 56-page opinion, Tostrud dismissed every claim brought by the Justice Department against Minnesota, Minneapolis, St. Paul and Hennepin County, concluding the challenged laws regulate only state and local officials, not the federal government.

DOJ ESCALATES BLUE-STATE ICE STANDOFF AFTER STATES REFUSE KEY FEDERAL REQUEST

"They do not command the federal government or its contractors to act. They do not forbid the federal government or its contractors from acting. They do not control how the federal government or its contractors undertake their work," Tostrud wrote. "Rather, they regulate how state and local officials perform their duties."

The ruling marks a significant setback for the administration's broader effort to block sanctuary policies across the country by arguing they unlawfully interfere with federal immigration enforcement.

But Eric Wessan, an attorney in the Iowa Solicitor General's Office, said he believed Tostrud's ruling conflicts with an earlier Eighth Circuit decision that he says gives the federal government stronger grounds to challenge state laws that interfere with federal immigration enforcement.

"States across the country have passed laws making state immigration crimes. The Eighth Circuit (which includes Minnesota) found one of those laws obstructed federal immigration enforcement, and so it was preempted," Wessan told Fox News Digital. "Judge Tostrud cited that opinion to explain that preemption is narrow. I think that his opinion is hard to square with the binding precedent."

FIRST ON FOX: DOJ SUES SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA OVER LAWS KNEECAPPING FEDERAL AGENTS AS MASK WAR ESCALATES

The Justice Department argued Minnesota's laws and local ordinances conflict with federal immigration statutes by restricting local officers from honoring ICE detainers, limiting information sharing with federal authorities and preventing local officials from participating in immigration enforcement.

But Tostrud concluded that accepting the administration's claim would create a constitutional problem under the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine.

The judge emphasized that while Congress possesses broad authority over immigration, it cannot compel states to use their own personnel and resources to carry out federal regulatory programs.

"The framers explicitly chose a Constitution that confers upon Congress the power to regulate individuals, not States," the opinion states, adding that the federal government "may not command the States' officers...to administer or enforce a federal regulatory program."

NEW YORK SHERIFFS 'MAD AS HELL' AS HOCHUL PUSHES TO BAN KEY LAW ENFORCEMENT PARTNERSHIP

Wessan agreed that states generally cannot be required to assist the federal government but argued the harder legal question is whether states can prohibit voluntary cooperation.

"States are not required to help the federal government enforce federal immigration law," he said. "Whether States can ban cooperation when certain actors (states or municipalities want to) is a harder question, and probably depends on the specific state and state laws."

Tostrud also rejected one of the administration's central arguments — that Minnesota's refusal to cooperate with ICE amounts to obstruction of federal immigration enforcement.

"Trefusing to help is not the same as impeding," Tostrud wrote.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Wessan argued the debate over that distinction distracts from the larger immigration crisis.

"The country is facing an immigration crisis," he said. "Rather than figuring out the fine line between impeding and refusing to help, Minnesota should appreciate the federal government's willingness to help with the illegal immigration crisis—and the waste, fraud, and abuse that accompanies it."

Minnesota leaders have defended the state's sanctuary-style policies, arguing they encourage immigrants in the country illegally to cooperate with local law enforcement by assuring them that reporting crimes or serving as witnesses will not automatically expose them to immigration enforcement.

The legal dispute also follows months of heightened immigration enforcement in Minnesota, where the Trump administration launched Operation Metro Surge, a large-scale ICE initiative that drew national attention, sparked protests and significantly increased the federal law enforcement presence across the state.

The operation intensified after two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by federal agents just weeks apart in January. Their deaths heightened scrutiny of Minnesota's immigration policies and prompted President Donald Trump to remove then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem from overseeing the operation, with border czar Tom Homan taking over the effort.

After taking over, Homan repeatedly argued that large-scale ICE operations would become less necessary if state and local officials cooperated with federal immigration authorities. Homan said that his "main focus now is drawdown," but stressed that reducing the federal presence would require greater cooperation from Minnesota officials.

"Cooperation with local authorities, especially jails and prisons, will give federal agents better access to people in the United States illegally. This would then lead to fewer federal law enforcement [agents] on Minnesota streets," Homan said.

Monday's ruling comes as the Trump administration continues to pursue similar lawsuits challenging sanctuary policies in several other states.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and the Justice Department for comment.

text:
(NewsNation) — The debate over why more Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers are not wearing body-worn cameras has only intensified since two deadly ICE shootings this month when federal officers working in Houston and Maine were not equipped with cameras.

Determining why all federal immigration agents and officers don’t have cameras that White House border czar Tom Homan says are essential to ICE operations and traffic stops, however, falls mainly along party lines, resulting in political finger-pointing.

Homan and Department of Homeland Security officials blame Democrats for significantly slowing the rollout of cameras to half of the nation’s 50 ICE field offices. Democrats, meanwhile, point to tens of billions of dollars in untapped federal funding that have been allocated for the purchase of cameras that have yet to be delivered.

How many ICE officers are wearing body-worn cameras?

A DHS spokesperson told NewsNation this week that body cameras have been deployed to more than half of the ICE field offices around the United States. The remaining offices, which include both ICE Emergency Removal Operations and Homeland Security Investigations locations, are expected to receive the cameras in less than 60 days.

The spokesperson did not specify where cameras were yet to be delivered, but elected officials in Houston and Maine said after the fatal shootings that they had been told that ICE officers in the respective field offices there would have cameras within 45 days.

DHS’s commitment of outfitting at least one person from each ICE arrest team with a camera comes six months after former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem wrote in a February social media post that cameras would be rapidly acquired and distributed across the U.S. after the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis “as funding is available.”

Former Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons testified on Capitol Hill in March that about 3,000 of 13,000 ICE officers were equipped with body cameras. At the same hearing, Customs and Border Protection Chief Rodney Scott testified that an testimated 10,000 of 20,000 Border Patrol agents working in the field were equipped with body cameras, saying that CBP is “building that program out.”

After the ninth fatal shooting involving a federal immigration officer or agent since President Donald Trump took office, Democrats and immigration advocates are seeking answers about the delays in getting body-worn cameras into the hands of officers working in the field on immigration enforcement.

A bipartisan group of members from the House Committee on Homeland Security was briefed on ongoing ICE operations by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin Wednesday as multiple federal investigations continue.

Committee Chair Andrew Garbarino, R-New York, told NewsNation that committee members received “timely answers” on the scheduling of body camera deployment, the training and vetting of new ICE officers as well as current guidance on ICE traffic stops.

The meeting comes a week after President Donald Trump overturned Mullin’s decision to pause most ICE traffic stops after the most recent fatal ICE shooting. The White House said that Trump and Mullin “are on the same page” about keeping ICE officers safe during enforcement operations.

Yet, while Garbarino says committee members remain focused on ensuring the safety of federal law enforcement and the public during ICE operations, some Democrats want faster deployment of more body cameras to officers without them.

“ICE has nearly infinite resources at its disposal — as well as enough funding for years — and yet this administration still sends ICE agents into the field without body cameras,” U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., said in a statement to USA Today. “In fact, ICE has had cameras in their possession for months that still haven’t been deployed to the field — they are purposely dragging their feet.”

Homan said this week that there is a schedule for cameras to be distributed and for training to begin. Without giving specifics about when all ICE officers would have the equipment, he said the training will include requirements for using the cameras, including when to turn them on and off and how long data should be stored on the cameras.

Asked when that process would be completed, Homan replied, “That’s a question for ICE.”

How much federal funding is available for ICE body-worn cameras?

Democrats maintain that Republicans have had more than $40 billion at their disposal for body cameras since Trump’s 2025 mega-spending bill. Instead, lawmakers such as Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., allege the Trump administration “blew tax dollars on private jets and gold-coated SUVs” rather than using funds allocated for ICE operations and to deploy body cameras.

Murray’s office points to $29.8 billion of the overall $75 billion earmarked specifically in Trump’s 2025 mega-bill for ICE to use as needed for ongoing agency operations. Another $10 billion within the bill was provided to the DHS secretary for “border support” that could have gone for body-worn cameras. The funding bill keeps federal immigration agencies funded through fiscal year 2029.

In addition, Congress separately earmarked $20 million specifically for body cameras as part of the annual DHS funding bill. But as of July 17, DHS had spent less than $75,000 of those funds on cameras, which Democrats argue puts gaping holes in their GOP counterparts’ arguments about who is to blame for the lack of ICE cameras being deployed around the country.

“The idea that Democrats are to blame for the Trump administration’s failure to deploy body cameras to the field and to protect people from out-of-control agents that they have failed to properly train is completely absurd,” Murray, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said in a statement to NewsNation this week.

“The problem has not been funding; ICE has more money than most modern militaries,” Murray said. “It’s been this administration’s refusal to quickly put in place basic accountability measures like requiring body cameras.”

Border czar wants Americans to witness what ICE officers are seeing in the field

Homan says he wants Americans “to see what that ICE agent sees when he takes action” during encounters between federal officers and those being sought as part of enforcement operations.

In the deaths of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Johan Sebastian Guerrero in Maine, neither of whom was the intended target of the ICE operation, the lack of body camera footage has refueled the ongoing controversy.

Specifically, concerns have arisen about why more federal law enforcement officers don’t have cameras and have not been trained on how to use them. Asked Monday for a timeline of when that could happen, Homan said, “As soon as possible if I had my way.”

Homan said body-worn cameras are “going to help ICE with the false media that’s out there.” However, when asked why Trump’s executive order revoking a previous order signed by former President Joe Biden that mandated the use of body-worn cameras came on the first anniversary of the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis, Homan replied, “That’s a question (for) above me”.

David Hernández, an associate professor of Latina/o Studies and Critical Race at Mount Holyoke College in Massachusetts, said that the DHS shutdown was not based on a lack of funding, but rather took place after the deaths of Good and Pretti and forced DHS to examine its operations.

As Homan and others pin blame for the camera delivery delay on Democrats, Hernández says administration officials are missing the mark. Instead, he said the shutdown came after intense scrutiny of a Minneapolis enforcement operation that Homan again acknowledged this week “wasn’t perfect.”

“It had nothing to do with the rollout of these (federal monies) because they had these monies,” Hernández told NewsNation.

He added, “I think (with) the finger-pointing, they’re (Republicans are) just trying to cover themselves. This is an administration that never admits wrong, that never admits weakness and always seeks to blame someone else for their own error.”

Why providing body cameras to all ICE officers won’t settle everything

Hernández, whose research centers on federal immigration operations, says even if ICE is fully stocked with body cameras, it likely will not lead to complete answers.

Although cameras can provide valuable footage, federal officers can often “narrate their own innocence” by getting phrases such as “stop resisting” into audio recordings, he said. That may lead to more conflicting accounts of encounters, Hernández said.

In some cases, ICE officers may not turn cameras on despite that being protocol, which could create more questions similar to those being asked in Houston and Maine, where no footage is available from the deadly encounters.

Hernández warns that although Homan is pushing for speedy delivery as more clamor for more federal officers to use the cameras, it may not deliver the results many are expecting.

“Even when there’s footage, there’s no accountability,” Hernández told NewsNation. “We’ve seen that in Minneapolis, where there’s footage of people being killed and still nothing happens. “So the body cameras aren’t a panacea in that sense.”

text:
ADDITIONAL MEDIA CONTACTS: James Woo, media@advancingjustice-atlanta.org; Desiree Evans, desiree@projectsouth.org

ATLANTA – On Friday, Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Atlanta, the ACLU of Georgia, and Project South filed a federal lawsuit against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement under the Freedom of Information Act. The lawsuit seeks records regarding the agency’s potential plans to expand immigration detention in Georgia and its use of the Atlanta ICE Field Office to detain immigrants. ICE has failed to provide these records despite its legal obligation to do so.

Advancing Justice - Atlanta requested records in February and May to obtain critical information that the public deserves to know about the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration tactics. The FOIA requests sought records related to ICE’s plans to convert large warehouses into mass detention centers in order to detain thousands more immigrants, including warehouses in Social Circle and Oakwood.

After months of community pressure, ICE has cancelled its plans to convert the warehouse in Social Circle into an immigrant detention center; but it has not yet confirmed its plans for the Oakwood warehouse.

Advancing Justice - Atlanta also sought records related to ICE’s use of its Atlanta Field Office Hold Room as a detention facility and the conditions there. In June 2025, ICE waived its long-standing policy limiting detention in field office hold rooms to 12 hours, allowing the agency to detain immigrants there for up to 72 hours. An investigation by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution found that ICE routinely held people for extended periods of time in the Atlanta Field Office Hold Room, even beyond 72 hours, and that immigrants lacked access to beds, showers, adequate medical care, or attorneys.

In March, our organizations sent a letter to ICE demanding that it stop holding immigrants in inhumane conditions at the Atlanta Field Office. ICE claimed it made meaningful improvements in response, but refused to provide proof of that. In an attempt to uncover the truth and hold ICE accountable, Advancing Justice – Atlanta requested detailed records about conditions inside the Atlanta ICE Hold Room.

ICE has failed to respond to these FOIA requests, so Advancing Justice – Atlanta, the ACLU of Georgia, and Project South have now filed this lawsuit to compel their release and to enforce ICE’s clear legal obligations to provide records to the public.

“ICE has acted with secrecy by keeping information from the public about the people it detains in the basement of the Atlanta ICE Field Office, as well as with its development of the warehouse detention centers. ICE can no longer cloak itself in darkness to insulate its unconscionable conduct from public scrutiny. We look forward to unearthing the truth about these important records,” said Samantha C. Hamilton, Senior Staff Attorney with Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Atlanta.

“It is appalling that ICE is going to such lengths to hide the truth. The public deserves to know about the inhumane conditions inside the Atlanta ICE Field Office holding cells where reports indicate individuals are held for days without proper food, beds, medical care, or access to counsel. ICE must be held accountable for all its destructive and deadly policies. We hope that this FOIA lawsuit will be the first step toward transparency and eventual accountability,” said Priyanka Bhatt, Senior Staff Attorney with Project South.

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services assisted the Department of Justice (DOJ) with several recent denaturalization actions in U.S. district courts to revoke citizenship from 10 individuals accused of serious crimes, including sexual abuse of a child, health care and wire fraud, immigration fraud, and conspiracy to possess cocaine with intent to distribute. The complaints were filed over the last 30 days.

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, a naturalized U.S. citizen’s citizenship may be revoked, and certificate of naturalization canceled, if the naturalization was illegally obtained or obtained by hiding important facts or by lying.

“When you commit fraud during the naturalization process, you forfeit the right to keep your U.S. citizenship,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “These criminal aliens, comprised of drug traffickers, pedophiles, and fraudsters, lost that right and exploited our immigration system—harming real U.S. citizens. DHS is committed to ensuring we denaturalize and remove these fraudsters with every tool at our disposal.”

Summary of Cases:

1. Yoskmaikel Rodriguez Perez (Age 45, Cuba): Rodriguez Perez became a lawful permanent resident in 2004 and a U.S. citizen in 2018. Before citizenship, he operated a fake medical clinic and submitted false claims to Medicare totaling more than $886,000. He hid these crimes during the naturalization process and gave false testimony under oath to a USCIS officer. He later pleaded guilty and was convicted of conspiracy to commit healthcare and wire fraud.

2. Ceflo Luviano-Mojica (Age 60, Mexico): On July 14, the United States filed a denaturalization action against Luviano-Mojica for hiding his prior arrest for carrying a concealed firearm and for grand theft, crimes for which he served 30 days in jail. In 1998, he pleaded guilty and was convicted in the Northern District of Georgia for providing false information in his naturalization application. He admitted to making false statements on his application and during his interview, testifying under oath that he had never been arrested, charged, or imprisoned for breaking or violating any law.

3. Urbano Vazquez Ortega (Age 53, Mexico): On July 10, the United States filed a denaturalization action against Vazquez Ortega, who became a U.S. citizen in 2017. He was convicted of multiple counts of second-degree child sexual abuse while employed as a priest at a Washington, D.C. church. In 2019, he was sentenced to 15 years in prison. The United States filed a five-count complaint seeking to revoke his citizenship, alleging he committed these crimes before, during, and after his naturalization.

4. Murtaza Ali (Age 65, Pakistan): Ali used multiple aliases to file several applications for immigration benefits, ultimately becoming a lawful permanent resident and then a U.S. citizen under the name “Muhammad Iqbal” in 2009. After naturalization, a fingerprint expert determined the fingerprints submitted under the names “Mortaza Ali” and “Muhammad Iqbal” belonged to the same person. The United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas charged Ali with making false statements to a U.S. agency. In 2014, Ali pleaded guilty, admitting that he had filed three applications using three different identities.

5. Jimmy Aguero (Age 51, Peru): Aguero repeatedly sexually abused his minor stepdaughter prior to becoming a U.S. citizen in 2015. He was convicted on eight counts of sexual abuse of a minor and sentenced to 10 years in prison. DOJ alleges Aguero is barred from establishing good moral character due to his convictions.

6. Antonio Alcantara-Ruiz (Age 53, Mexico): On June 23, the United States filed a denaturalization action against Alcantara-Ruiz, also known as Emiliano Quintana-Gonzalez and Antonio Quinn Alcantara, for misrepresenting his identity to secure citizenship. Before naturalization, he purchased identity documents from another Mexican citizen and used them to obtain a replacement permanent resident card with his own photograph and fingerprint. He used these false documents to support his naturalization application.

7. Omar Cantu-Montalvo (Age 44, Mexico): Cantu-Montalvo was admitted to the United States in 1996 and later became a lawful permanent resident. He applied for citizenship in July 2005, stating he had never committed a crime for which he had been arrested. He naturalized in December 2005. In April 2016, he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to possess more than five kilograms of cocaine with intent to distribute—a conspiracy he joined in April 2005, just months before applying for citizenship. He was sentenced to 100 months in prison and five years of supervised release.

8. Franscisco Montano (Age 59, Mexico): Montano was admitted to the United States in 1987. When he applied for citizenship in 1997, he failed to disclose that he had sexually abused a child during the required five-year good moral character period before naturalization. He was later convicted in a Texas state court of two counts of aggravated sexual assault and four counts of indecency with a child, crimes that occurred during that five-year period.

9. Marcin Stanislaw Garbacz (Age 47, Poland): Garbacz, a former Roman Catholic priest, became a lawful permanent resident in 2008 and a U.S. citizen in 2014. Before citizenship, he stole about $259,696 in cash collections from three parishes in South Dakota and secretly recorded a 17-year-old showering during a church trip to Poland. He hid these crimes during the naturalization process. He was convicted of wire fraud, filing a false tax return, and engaging in illicit sexual conduct with a minor in a foreign country.

10. Martin Garcia Cardiel (Age 60, Mexico): On July 6, the United States filed a complaint in Utah to revoke Garcia Cardiel’s citizenship. He was admitted to the United States in December 2000 and later became a lawful permanent resident. In his 2011 citizenship application, he stated that he had never committed a crime for which he had been arrested and had never given false information to any U.S. government official. He naturalized in October 2011. In 2022, a Utah jury convicted him of 19 counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child for acts committed in 2007. The victims were his neighbors, two sisters who were 7 and 8 years old when the abuse began. He was sentenced to consecutive prison terms of 15 years to life.

The Department of Justice has filed complaints seeking to revoke citizenship for these individuals. The crimes they committed show they lacked the good moral character required to become a U.S. citizen, and they lied to USCIS officers to hide these crimes during their naturalization interviews.

These complaints were filed in the Southern District of Florida, Northern District of Georgia, Southern District of Iowa, District of Maryland, Western District of Pennsylvania, Northern District of Texas, Southern District of Texas, Southern District of Texas, District of Utah, and Western District of Washington. The claims made in the complaints are allegations only, and there has been no determination of liability.

To report suspected immigration benefit fraud or abuse to USCIS, please use the USCIS Tip Form.

text:
On July 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts issued an administrative stay temporarily preventing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) from implementing certain agency policies adopted to carry out portions of H.R. 1 (the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”) while the court considers plaintiffs’ request for a stay pending judicial review. The challenged policies would have retroactively affected the employment authorization of certain Temporary Protected Status (TPS) beneficiaries and asylum applicants beginning July 22, 2026. The order is expected to have its most immediate impact on TPS beneficiaries whose employment authorization was subject to USCIS’s July 22 implementation guidance, including beneficiaries from several TPS-designated countries.

In Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts v. USCIS, No. 1:26-cv-13038 (D. Mass. July 21, 2026), Judge Nathaniel Gorton concluded that an administrative stay was warranted because many TPS beneficiaries faced the imminent loss of work authorization beginning July 22, 2026, while asylum applicants faced rejection of applications and other potentially severe consequences before the court could fully consider the legality of the challenged policies. The administrative stay will remain in effect until the court rules on the plaintiffs’ motion for a stay under the Administrative Procedure Act, which the court indicated will occur no later than August 5, 2026.

What the Court Order Does

The court temporarily stayed USCIS’s implementation of the following policies:

Retroactively shortening the validity of certain Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) held by TPS beneficiaries that would otherwise expire under USCIS’s implementation of H.R. 1;

Rejecting asylum applications solely because the applicant failed to pay the newly imposed annual asylum application fee;

Terminating employment authorization based on nonpayment of the annual asylum application fee; and

Initiating removal proceedings solely because an asylum applicant failed to pay the annual asylum application fee.

As a result, affected TPS beneficiaries may continue to rely on the employment authorization expiration dates that applied before USCIS’s retroactive implementation of the challenged policies while the administrative stay remains in effect. The order restores the prior expiration dates; it does not create a new extension of employment authorization.

What Remains in Effect

The court did not stay all aspects of USCIS’s implementation of H.R. 1. Specifically, USCIS may continue to:

Collect the new annual asylum application fee; and

Process initial asylum-based employment authorization applications without the prior 30-day adjudication timeline that had been eliminated by the April 2026 interim final rule.

Employer Considerations

Employers with employees working pursuant to TPS should be aware that this order temporarily pauses USCIS’s retroactive implementation of certain work authorization limitations affecting TPS beneficiaries and asylum applicants subject to the challenged policies. The decision provides important short-term relief but does not resolve the underlying legal challenge.

Form I-9 Considerations

Employers should avoid taking adverse employment action based solely on the July 22, 2026 employment authorization expiration dates established under the challenged USCIS policies while the administrative stay remains in effect. Employers should continue to monitor USCIS guidance and consult counsel regarding affected employees because the stay is temporary and may be modified or dissolved following further court proceedings.

Because the court has not yet ruled on the plaintiffs’ underlying request for a stay pending judicial review, employers should continue to closely monitor developments before taking employment eligibility actions based solely on the recently announced H.R. 1 implementation guidance.

WR Immigration is actively monitoring this litigation and will provide additional updates as the case progresses.

title: 'Where Do We Go from Here': Forward or Backward? - The Texas Observer
description:
They were always sinking deeper in debt, deeper in poverty, and deeper in a system designed to keep Black families from getting ahead.
The ruling weakened a key section of the Voting Rights Act, a law that has helped protect minority voters for decades.
When citizens vote, serve on juries, attend public meetings, contact elected officials, and engage in civic life, they help shape the future of their communities.
James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered in 1964 while helping Black citizens register to vote in Mississippi.
Will we move forward toward a nation where opportunity is expanded and every citizen’s voice is heard, or will we move backward toward a time when access, representation, and participation were reserved for only some Americans?
text:
My parents lived through Jim Crow. Around our dinner table, they told stories that sounded impossible to me as a child. They talked about not being allowed to eat in certain restaurants, or even to try on clothes or shoes before buying them. My father often spoke about growing up in a sharecropping family. At the end of each year, he would watch tears run down my grandfather’s face as they rode home in their wagon after settling accounts with the landowner. Despite a year’s worth of backbreaking labor, they always seemed to owe more than they had earned. They had been cheated again. They were always sinking deeper in debt, deeper in poverty, and deeper in a system designed to keep Black families from getting ahead.

These stories aren’t ancient history; they happened within my parents’ lifetimes. As the child of people who endured many other injustices, and in light of today’s fights over voting rights and representation, I feel compelled to ask whether the hard-won progress, which so many Americans bled for, is being protected, or slowly eroded by recent decisions that restrict the vote and dilute political voices.

Although legal segregation was dismantled decades ago, the struggle for full participation in American democracy did not end. The civil rights movement secured historic victories, including the Voting Rights Act of 1965, but each generation has faced new debates about access to the ballot, political representation, and whose voices are heard in the democratic process.

In April, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a major voting-rights decision in Louisiana v. Callais. The ruling weakened a key section of the Voting Rights Act, a law that has helped protect minority voters for decades. As a result, states have greater freedom to redraw political districts in ways that dilute the voting power of Black communities and limit their voice in government.

That debate is not only taking place in Washington; it is unfolding here in Texas. State lawmakers recently approved House Bill 4, a congressional redistricting plan signed by Governor Greg Abbott. Supporters said the measure ensures fair representation, while critics argued it redraws district lines in ways that could reduce the political influence of Black and Latino voters and make it harder for some communities to elect candidates of their choice. Such changes arguably reduced the number of districts in which Black voters held sway. For example, Al Green, a Democrat, long represented Texas’ 9th Congressional District. Under the new map passed by Texas lawmakers, most of his current constituents were shifted into the redrawn 18th Congressional District, where Green ran, but lost to another Black congressman, who formerly would not have been his competitor.

As America marks its 250th year, the question remains: Are we committed to continuing to build a more inclusive democracy, or are we willing to accept the erosion of the protections previous generations fought so hard to secure?

Regardless of where one stands on individual issues, the larger challenge remains: How can we ensure that every eligible citizen has both the opportunity and the confidence to participate fully in our democracy? The answer matters because political participation is the foundation of self-government. When citizens vote, serve on juries, attend public meetings, contact elected officials, and engage in civic life, they help shape the future of their communities. When participation declines, democracy itself becomes weaker.

My parents understood something that many Americans today have never experienced: Rights can be denied, opportunities can be taken away, and progress is never guaranteed. The barriers they faced did not disappear on their own. They were challenged by ordinary citizens who organized, protested, voted, went to court, and in some cases gave their lives so that future generations could enjoy freedoms that had previously been denied.

The rights and opportunities we Americans now enjoy were not freely given; they were won through struggle and sacrifice. Civil rights leader Fannie Lou Hamer was evicted and lost her job for trying to register to vote and later jailed and beaten after sitting at an all-white lunch counter in the 1960s. Medgar Evers was assassinated in 1963 for his civil rights work. James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered in 1964 while helping Black citizens register to vote in Mississippi. Their stories remind us that the right to vote is sacred because it gives citizens a voice in determining who governs them and whether that government represents their interests fairly.

In 1967, the year before his assassination, Martin Luther King Jr. published Where Do We Go from Here: Chaos or Community? In that book, he challenged America to move beyond the legal victories of the civil rights movement and confront the deeper structures of inequality. King warned, “We are now faced with the fact that tomorrow is today. We are confronted with the fierce urgency of now.”

Nearly 60 years later, King’s question remains just as urgent. Will we move forward toward a nation where opportunity is expanded and every citizen’s voice is heard, or will we move backward toward a time when access, representation, and participation were reserved for only some Americans?

The answer will not be decided by courts alone, nor by legislatures, nor by presidents. It will be decided by citizens. Every generation inherits the unfinished work of democracy. The direction we choose today will determine whether our children and grandchildren tell stories of progress preserved or hard-won rights lost around their own dinner tables.

text:
Last month, the Policy & Advocacy team launched Their Future, Their Voice: Centering Displaced Children in Global Protection and Policy. Developed in partnership with refugee-led and community-based organizations, the report brings together recommendations from child protection practitioners, refugee leaders, and analysts, calling for stronger protections for displaced children, greater investment in essential services, meaningful youth participation in decision-making, and sustained support for local and refugee-led organizations. Dedicated to young people living through displacement, the report also features their artwork and poetry throughout. Read the full report here.

Since our last newsletter, the policy team and USCRI published initial reporting on conditions in Haiti, issued a statement on the Supreme Court’s Temporary Protected Status decision, and penned a reflection on refugees’ and immigrants’ role in America at 250. Also, don’t miss this interview Rachel Ryu, Staff Attorney with USCRI Humanitarian Legal Services, had with Milagro Sique, CEO of Dorcas International Institute of Rhode Island, discussing Dorcas’ decision to join a federal court lawsuit challenging these USCIS policies.

The work of USCRI’s Policy and Advocacy team is only possible with support from people like you — please consider supporting our work today to help us continue advancing protections and solutions for refugees and immigrants worldwide. Thank you!

Read the newsletter here

Featured Brief

On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court fundamentally altered the future of Temporary Protected Status (TPS). In a 6-3 decision in Mullin v. Doe, the Court allowed the Trump administration to move forward in ending TPS for Syria and Haiti, while limiting the ability of federal courts to review whether those decisions complied with statutory requirements. While the ruling did not eliminate the TPS program itself, it significantly expanded the federal government’s ability to terminate TPS designations for most countries while legal challenges continue, leaving hundreds of thousands of people in legal limbo.

When the case was argued before the Supreme Court on April 29, 2026, USCRI warned that the outcome could threaten the stability of nearly 1.3 million people protected under TPS. With the Court’s decision, we may now see one of the largest de- documentation events in U.S. history. This decision has deepened uncertainty for hundreds of thousands of TPS holders, many of whom have built lives, raised families, and strengthened communities across the United States over decades.

title: DHS Ends “Duration of Status” for F Students and J Exchange Visitors - Honigman LLP
description:
Effective September 15, 2026, F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants will no longer be admitted to the U.S. for D/S.
This alert summarizes the key changes and highlights practical considerations for employers that recruit or employ F-1 and J-1 visa holders.
Key Considerations for Employers I-94 Tracking and I-9 Compliance.
Employers that recruit F-1 students through OPT or STEM OPT should account for additional filing and approval time.
Bottom Line for Employers Track I-94 expiration dates for all F-1 and J-1 employees, in addition to SEVIS program end dates and EAD expiration dates.
text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) recently published a final rule that will replace “duration of status” (D/S) admissions for F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors with fixed I-94 expiration dates, creating new timing considerations for employers that recruit or employ these individuals. Effective September 15, 2026, F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants will no longer be admitted to the U.S. for D/S. Instead, these individuals generally will receive an I-94 with a fixed admission end date based on the length of their program, up to a maximum period of four years. Foreign nationals who wish to remain in the U.S. in F-1 or J-1 status beyond that date must apply for an extension of stay (EOS) with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), or depart and seek readmission, to avoid accruing unlawful presence. This alert summarizes the key changes and highlights practical considerations for employers that recruit or employ F-1 and J-1 visa holders.

What is the New Rule?

F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants historically have been admitted into the U.S. for D/S, meaning they could remain in the U.S. for the time required to complete their program and any authorized post-completion employment, provided they continued to comply with the terms and conditions of their nonimmigrant classification. For F-1 students, this period included a 60-day departure grace period. For J-1 exchange visitors, it included a 30-day departure grace period. Because there was no fixed admission end date, F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants generally did not need to file an EOS with USCIS when a program or post-completion employment period lasted longer than expected. Instead, the school or exchange program sponsor updated the individual’s SEVIS record and issued an updated Form I-20 or DS-2019.

Beginning September 15, 2026, F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants will be admitted into the U.S. for a fixed period with a specific end date. The admission period will be based on the program length listed on the Form I-20 or DS-2019 and generally will be capped at four years. Shorter admission periods will apply to certain categories, including individuals enrolled in English language programs, attending public high school, or commuting across the border. F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants will receive 30-day arrival and departure grace periods; neither grace period will count against the four-year maximum admission period. For F-1 students, this represents a reduction from the current 60-day departure grace period. If an F-1 or J-1 nonimmigrant requires additional time to complete a program or engage in authorized activity, the individual must file an EOS with USCIS before the fixed admission period expires.

How Does the New Rule Impact Current F and J Nonimmigrants?

Individuals holding F-1 or J-1 status when the new rule takes effect may remain in the U.S. until the later date of:

the current program end date listed on the individual’s Form I-20 or DS-2019;

the end of any post-completion OPT or STEM OPT that is valid on the rule’s effective date; or

four years from the effective date (September 15, 2030), whichever is earlier, plus the applicable departure grace period (60 days for F nonimmigrants, 30 days for J nonimmigrants).

If these individuals travel internationally after the rule takes effect, they will receive a new fixed-admission I-94 upon re-entry. Individuals who wish to remain in the U.S. beyond the applicable end point, including to begin a new program of study or engage in post-completion OPT or STEM OPT, must file an EOS with USCIS or travel and seek readmission with a new period of admission.

Notably, F-1 students who have a pending OPT or STEM OPT EAD application when the rule takes effect, or who file an OPT or STEM OPT EAD application on or before March 18, 2027 (six months after the effective date), will not need to file a separate EOS for the requested period of OPT or STEM OPT.

Key Considerations for Employers

I-94 Tracking and I-9 Compliance. Because F-1 and J-1 employees will now have a date-certain I-94 that will govern how long the individual is authorized to remain in the U.S., employers should update immigration tracking systems to monitor I-94 expiration dates alongside SEVIS program end dates and EAD expiration dates. For I-9 purposes, when an F-1 employee has timely filed an EOS, the employee’s I-94 or EAD, as applicable, combined with a USCIS receipt notice (Form I-797) confirming the pending EOS, may be treated as unexpired for up to 240 days. Employers should work with counsel to confirm the specific documentation combinations that satisfy I-9 reverification requirements under the new framework.

Recruiting and Onboarding. Employers that recruit F-1 students through OPT or STEM OPT should account for additional filing and approval time. Going forward, students seeking post-completion OPT generally will need to file both an EOS application (Form I-539) and an employment authorization application (Form I-765) with USCIS. Students may not begin new post-completion OPT employment until both applications are approved. This dual-filing requirement may create additional lead time between graduation and work authorization. Employers should build additional time into offer timelines, start-date planning, and onboarding communications. Employers also should coordinate closely with candidates and their designated school officials (DSOs) on filing deadlines. Concurrent filing of Forms I-539 and I-765 is permitted and recommended.

H-1B Cap-Gap. The rule does not modify the existing H-1B cap-gap provisions. F-1 students who are beneficiaries of timely filed, cap-subject H-1B petitions requesting a change of status will continue to receive an automatic extension of F-1 status and any associated employment authorization through April 1 of the applicable fiscal year, or the start date of the approved H-1B petition, whichever is earlier. Employers should still evaluate H-1B sponsorship and cap-gap strategy earlier in the employment lifecycle because fixed I-94 dates may create additional timing pressure.

Potential Litigation. Employers should be aware that the rule may face legal challenges. A prior version of this rulemaking was proposed in 2020 and subsequently withdrawn, and the 2025 proposed rule drew significant opposition, including from a coalition of state attorneys general. Employers should prepare for compliance by the September 15, 2026 effective date as currently scheduled, while also monitoring for judicial developments that could delay or alter implementation.

Bottom Line for Employers

Track I-94 expiration dates for all F-1 and J-1 employees, in addition to SEVIS program end dates and EAD expiration dates.

Build I-9 reverification reminders around fixed I-94 dates and timely filed EOS applications.

Plan earlier for OPT, STEM OPT, and H-1B sponsorship timelines.

Identify affected employees before September 15, 2026, and communicate filing and travel risks.

Monitor litigation or agency guidance that could delay or change implementation.

text:
A federal judge has ordered the release of a woman arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Logan Airport when she was trying to fly home from a Noah Kahan concert in Boston.

Maria Rosales, a 32-year-old mother from Colombia, was one of two people ICE arrested at the airport on July 10, according to the agency and immigration attorney Todd Pomerleau.

Judge Myong J. Joun said Monday that Rosales had to be released by 7 p.m. that day and allowed to go home to Miami. Pomerleau confirmed Tuesday that she was free from custody.

"Respondents have failed to demonstrate compliance with the statutory and regulatory procedures governing Petitioner's detention," Joun wrote. "The appropriate remedy is release, under reasonable conditions pending further proceedings."

He added that a condition preventing her from returning to her home "would be unreasonable."

Pomerleau, who represents Rosales, said she is a recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals and does not have a criminal record. He explained that she was initially brought to the U.S. at the age of 4 and that her latest DACA renewal has stalled for three years.

"She's traumatized, because what the government is now claiming, which she didn't know, is they're claiming she missed a court hearing when she was much younger," he told NBC10 Boston last week. "But she got DACA that same year."

An ICE spokesperson told NBC10 Boston that Rosales overstayed a visitor visa after entering the U.S. in 1998. The spokesperson, who did not mention DACA, said an immigration judge ordered her removal in June of 2017 — the year Pomerleau said she became a DACA recipient.

Last month, immigrant advocacy and legal aid groups sued the Trump administration, demanding answers about such delays. Asked about the lawsuit at the time, a Department of Homeland Security told NBC News that DACA recipients "are not automatically protected from deportations."

Joun said the federal government must not detain her again "absent compliance with the applicable statutory and regulatory procedures."

Pomerleau said Tuesday that Rosales is happy to be out, but remains traumatized by the experience.

David Ardila, another client of Pomerleau's, was arrested by ICE the same day. An ICE spokesperson said both arrests happened "during targeted operations at Boston Logan Airport."

Pomerleau said the 33-year-old is a native of Venezuela who has an asylum petition and flew in from Seattle to attend a World Cup match.

ICE told NBC10 Boston Ardila entered on a visa in 2017 and overstayed "for over eight years in violation of the terms of his lawful admission." The spokesperson did not mention an asylum claim.

"Neither person has a criminal record. They're both traveling for leisure," the attorney said last week.

Read the full statement ICE shared last week:

On July 10, ICE Boston arrested two illegal aliens during targeted operations at Boston Logan Airport.

Maria Rosales, an illegal alien from Colombia, entered the United States on September 7, 1998, under a visitor visa that allowed her to stay in the country until March 6, 1999. Rosales was ordered removed by an immigration judge on June 28, 2017. She has illegally overstayed her visa and remained in the country for over eight years since being ordered removed.

David Ricardo Ardila Valero, an illegal alien from Venezuela, entered the United States on May 11, 2017, under a visa that allowed him to stay in the country until Nov. 10, 2017. He overstayed his visa and remained in the United States illegally for over eight years in violation of the terms of his lawful admission.

Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.
