text:
Jesus Hernandez Ortiz, 38, of Puerto Rico, pleaded guilty today in the District of Vermont to one count of conspiracy to illegally bring aliens to the United States and one count of illegally bringing at least one alien to the United States for the purpose of private financial gain.

Hernandez Ortiz and a co-defendant, Francisco Antonio Luna Rosado, were charged on Jan. 29. According to court documents, as early as September 2023, Hernandez Ortiz was added to an encrypted chat platform that coordinated drivers for long distance trips, including the pick-up of aliens illegally crossing into the United States from Canada. In mid-September 2023, Hernandez Ortiz agreed to such a trip. Hernandez Ortiz rented a commercial van in New Jersey and drove the van to the designated pick-up location in Holland, Vermont, at the assigned time. Hernandez Ortiz’s co-conspirators updated him on the exact location and time of the pick-up. Once there, Hernandez Ortiz picked up a group of twelve, including two young children, who had just entered the United States illegally. Hernandez Ortiz expected payment of $400 per alien ($4,800 total) upon arrival in New York City.

Images of the rented Home Depot van, which Hernandez drove during a smuggling event, that law enforcement stopped. Text messages between Luna Rosado (left side in blue) and Hernandez (right side in green), with translations into English, discussing the alleged smuggling operation.

“The defendant joined a sophisticated illegal alien smuggling network, which spanned at least three continents, and even smuggled young children,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Smuggling illegal aliens over our borders — whether southern or northern — puts both aliens and the American people at risk and violates the sanctity of our laws and our national security. The Department of Justice will continue to aggressively prosecute alien smugglers to enforce our criminal laws against illegal immigration and keep the American people safe.”

“The northern border is incredibly dangerous and anyone encouraging or facilitating the smuggling of aliens, especially children, across the border in these remote locations is putting lives at risk,” said Acting Deputy Executive Associate Director Matthew Millhollin of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). “Hernandez Ortiz has admitted to smuggling aliens for profit and now he’s facing real prison time. HSI and our law enforcement partners are using intelligence-focused investigations to secure our borders and stop alien smugglers in their tracks.”

The Swanton Sector Intelligence Unit assigned to the U.S. Border Patrol Newport Station and the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) New England Office led U.S. investigative efforts, with assistance from HSI’s Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C. and CBP’s National Targeting Center International Interdiction Task Force.

Trial Attorneys Jake Drucker and Emily Cohen of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, Trial Attorney Alexandra Skinnion of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Eugenia Cowles for the District of Vermont are prosecuting the case.

The Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section's (MNF) mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

MNF’s Money Laundering and Forfeiture Unit investigates and prosecutes sophisticated money laundering schemes involving financial facilitators, gatekeepers, and other individuals and entities laundering criminal proceeds, and litigates complex civil forfeiture cases to recover assets on behalf of victims.

The investigation and charges are supported and prosecuted by Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA), the Department’s lead effort in combating high-impact human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations (TCOs). A highly successful partnership between the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes human smuggling and trafficking and related immigration crimes that impact public safety and border security. JTFA’s mission is to target the leaders and organizers of Cartels and TCOs involved in human smuggling and trafficking throughout the Americas. The Attorney General has elevated and expanded JTFA to target the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking groups operating not only in Mexico and the Northern Triangle countries of Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras, but also in Canada, the Caribbean and the maritime border, and elsewhere. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by the Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, the Office of International Affairs, and the Office of Enforcement Operations, among others, JTFA has dedicated Assistant United States Attorney-detailees from the Southern District of California; District of Arizona; District of New Mexico; Western and Southern Districts of Texas; Southern District of Florida; Northern District of New York; and District of Vermont. JTFA also partners with other USAOs throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS, including ICE/ HSI and CBP/BP and OFO, as well as FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 465 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and/or trafficking; more than 419 U.S. convictions; more than 363 significant jail sentences imposed, and forfeitures of substantial assets.

text:
A dozen progressive aldermen have signed on to a demand for their colleagues to reject contributions from corporations tied to federal immigration enforcement, in the latest political fallout over the recent U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement presence in Chicago.

The “ICE Out of Chicago Elections” campaign debuted on Tuesday with 12 members of the City Council’s Progressive Caucus joining the pledge to refuse all future contributions from a list of corporations and political committees they say “enable brutal immigration enforcement tactics.”

The campaign, aimed at other members of the council, comes after last fall’s Operation Midway Blitz pummeled Chicago with aggressive deportations and sparked citywide grassroots demonstrations against ICE as well as U.S Customs and Border Protection.

The immigration crackdown also became a cudgel in the Democratic primaries this March, when the party’s left and moderate wings fought over how leadership can best stand up to President Donald Trump.

“This immigration enforcement campaign is only possible with the assistance of private industry,” the pledge reads. “Private companies profit by providing agents with housing, cars, technology, and more. Some of those same companies want to curry favor in Chicago’s elections and win more government contracts that use our tax dollars.”

The eleven companies and one PAC singled out by “ICE Out of Chicago” are: Motorola Solutions, Waste Management and Stericycle, Target, SP+Parking, Home Depot, Amazon, FedEx, Microsoft, Dell, Deloitte, Ean Holdings (Enterprise, National and Alamo) and the Illinois Hotel & Motel PAC. For the last name, the pledge says Marriott and Hilton “allow immigration agents to stay at their properties.” The list can change depending on the companies’ contracts and policies.

The ICE Out campaign was organized by an existing local group in support of the Chicago Fair Elections Ordinance, which would allow political campaigns to benefit from public funding. Members of that coalition include the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, Reform for Illinois, the League of Women Voters of Chicago, The People’s Lobby and Asian American Midwest Progressives.

“Chicagoans, like many Americans, are paying close attention to how elected officials respond to ICE’s actions and Trump’s dangerous immigration agenda,” Ald. Anthony Quezada, 35th, told the Tribune in a statement. “Voters want leaders who are willing to stand up for our communities and act consistently with their values. That’s why I believe many Chicagoans will expect their representatives to reject contributions from companies that support or profit from ICE and Border Patrol operations.”

Though the White House’s deportation tactics have been widely unpopular in Chicago, Democrats have differed on how to respond.

Some candidates on the left have taken stronger stances in an effort to distinguish themselves as fierce opponents of Trump — such as when Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Juliana Stratton embraced the “Abolish ICE” movement and hammered her primary opponent U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi for a past contribution tied to Palantir Technologies, which has contracts with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

In the City Council, moderates have countered that local government does not have the authority to fully stop Trump’s actions, and officials should focus on finding common ground with the federal government rather than antagonize it. Mayor Brandon Johnson, for his part, has signed a spate of executive orders aimed at reigning in DHS including and up to directing Chicago police to investigate federal agents for misconduct, though no such criminal case has been brought forth for charges yet.

Last week, the Tribune also reported that downtown Ald. Bill Conway has a financial stake in the contractor that runs ICE’s biggest detention camp. GrizzlyRock Capital LLC, a private investment firm, has $7.5 million invested in Amentum Holdings, a massive government contractor that now runs Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas, according to a Tribune analysis.

Kyle Mowery, GrizzlyRock’s manager, is a close political ally of Conway’s and contributed $52,000 to his campaigns, campaign finance records show.

In response, a Conway spokesperson said the 34th Ward alderman had been unaware of the GrizzlyRock investment in Amentum and “recommended that GrizzlyRock sell their shares because they should not be invested in a company helping carry out the Trump administration’s reprehensible immigration actions.”

title: ICE killed a man in Houston and residents want answers. But Trump's gerrymander may ...
description:
Despite Garcia’s efforts, East End residents face an uphill battle to get answers from the Trump administration and hold ICE accountable.
That’s because, thanks to President Donald Trump’s nationwide push for pro-GOP partisan redistricting, many are set to lose their voice in Congress.
In 2024, District 29 — which included the East End — voted for Kamala Harris by 20 points.
But after November, many of her former constituents in the East End will no longer have her voice advocating for them.
In Houston, the Harris County District Attorney’s office has begun an independent investigation into the ICE shooting, but it’s clear that it will be a struggle.
text:
When Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant, in Houston earlier this month, Rep. Sylvia Garcia (D) sprang into action.

Garcia immediately questioned the immigration agency’s account of the incident and demanded an independent investigation. She rushed to gather firsthand accounts of the shooting, meeting with witnesses who were in federal custody at an immigration detention facility. When security officers initially insisted she could not enter, Garcia was undeterred.

“The victim’s family, my constituents, and the entire community deserve a complete and transparent accounting of what happened,” Garcia said in a statement.

In demanding accountability, Garcia is fulfilling an essential component of her job as a member of Congress: representing the people of the heavily Latino East End — including the Magnolia Park neighborhood where the shooting took place — and ensuring that her constituents’ voices are heard in the halls of power.

Despite Garcia’s efforts, East End residents face an uphill battle to get answers from the Trump administration and hold ICE accountable. But starting next year, their odds are likely to be even steeper.

That’s because, thanks to President Donald Trump’s nationwide push for pro-GOP partisan redistricting, many are set to lose their voice in Congress.

When Texas redrew its congressional map last year under pressure from Trump, lawmakers split the East End in two, putting parts of it, including the Magnolia Park area, into a new Republican-leaning 9th District. After the November elections, it will likely have a GOP congresswoman who has said almost nothing about Salgado Araujo’s killing.

The episode is perhaps the starkest recent example of how Trump’s gerrymanders aren’t just boosting the GOP’s chances of retaining control of Congress. They also damage democracy on an even more fundamental level — by undermining the ability of voters, especially minority voters, to elect leaders who will truly represent their interests and respond to their concerns — even in matters of life and death.

Shifting borders, shifting reality

East End voters redrawn into the new District 9 will have two options on the ballot in November: Democrat Leticia Gutierrez and Republican Alex Mealer.

Gutierrez is an immigrant and public health advocate who has lived in the district for most of her life. Mealer is an Army veteran who filed a 2023 lawsuit challenging the results of a local election she lost. (Even Mealer’s own lawyer said she didn’t support Mealer’s claims of fraud.) And Mealer’s opponent in the GOP primary blasted her for not living in the district.

Since Salgado Araujo’s killing, Mealer has said little about the case.

Her only statement was in a social media post on the day of the shooting, when she shared information from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that amplified ICE’s version of events.

“Today is yet another reminder of the dangers law enforcement face everyday as they protect our safety,” Mealer wrote. “I have full confidence in law enforcement’s ability to conduct a thorough investigation and ensure justice is served.”

In response, Gutierrez posted a video criticizing Mealer’s response and drawing a direct line between the redistricting scheme and Mealer’s stance on the shooting. Her conclusion: “They redrew this district to silence the East End.”

‘Pawns’ in the redistricting fight

Though debates over redistricting often focus on who controls Congress, Houstonians will now face the wider consequences voting advocates warned of last year.

Gerrymander opponents repeatedly sounded the alarm that Republicans redrew Texas’ congressional map at the expense of minority voters — and particularly of Latino Texans. They account for much of the state’s population growth over the past decade, yet stand to lose representation under the new map.

In a court filing challenging the gerrymander, advocates pointed out that all eight of the districts most impacted by the changes had majority-minority populations.

Richard Murray, a political scientist at the University of Houston who has analyzed Texas political trends for decades, testified in federal court that the new map makes profound and unnecessary changes to longstanding Houston congressional districts that have been electing minority representatives for decades. It amounts to “evidence of intentional discrimination,” he said. (A federal court found likely intentional discrimination and blocked the map, but the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately reversed the ruling.)

State Sen. Royce West (D), who also testified against the map, told the court that there’s a predictable outcome when Texas Republicans redraw a map for political gain: “It’s always the minority communities that end up being the pawns.”

And the shift will be extreme.

In 2024, District 29 — which included the East End — voted for Kamala Harris by 20 points. Under the new map, a large portion of the neighborhood is now part of a newly formed district, District 9, that stretches out into rural Liberty County, and that Mealer is favored to win.

Garcia told reporters Tuesday that she’s heard from community members who are worried about the changes.

“I know that many of the constituents that I have in the current 29th Congressional District are saddened,” she said. “They’re concerned because they’re just not sure that they’re going to be able to compete, particularly with northern parts of the district that go all the way to Liberty County, whether they’ll be able to compete with it for the time and attention of a new member.”

New representation

For her part, Garcia isn’t going anywhere: She is running for re-election in the new District 29.

But after November, many of her former constituents in the East End will no longer have her voice advocating for them. And fighting ICE’s impunity requires playing the long game.

Minneapolis officials have been struggling for more than six months to hold ICE accountable for the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, making slow progress in the face of long odds.

In Houston, the Harris County District Attorney’s office has begun an independent investigation into the ICE shooting, but it’s clear that it will be a struggle.

Two weeks after the incident, DHS officials still have not even disclosed the names of the ICE officers involved. Aaron Reitz, the new U.S. attorney for southern Texas, is a far-right backer of Trump’s mass deportation agenda. He has called for the federal government to deport “as many [immigrants] as possible” and threatened to denaturalize political opponents.

Mealer did not respond to detailed questions from Democracy Docket asking her whether she would continue efforts to hold ICE accountable for Salgado Araujo’s shooting death, whether she lives in the district and whether she believes the immigration agency’s aggressive tactics violated policy.

However, Gutierrez, her Democratic opponent, did respond.

“If elected, I will continue Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia’s fight to demand answers, accountability, and justice for the family of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo,” Gutierrez said in a statement. “No family should have to bury a loved one without knowing the truth, and no federal agency should ever be above accountability.”

Salgado Araujo’s killing “raises deeply troubling questions that demand an independent investigation,” Gutierrez continued.

“To every resident of District 9, especially those living in mixed-status households, I want you to hear this: you deserve to live with dignity, not fear. I want our neighbors to know they are not alone,” Gutierrez added. “And to everyone who is eligible to vote this November: your voice matters. Change only happens when ordinary people stand together and demand it.”

title: US Senate Dems press Mullin to ensure all immigration agents have body cameras
description:
The lawmakers pressed Mullin about providing body cameras to immigration officers, pointing out the Congress has allocated $175 billion to the department since last year.
None of the ICE officers involved in the shootings were wearing body cameras.
Among Democrats’ demands at the time was that immigration officers wear body cameras.
Top Trump officials, including then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, said body cameras would be provided to immigration agents.
During the second Trump administration, federal immigration officers have shot 22 people and killed six, including three U.S. citizens.
text:
WASHINGTON — A supermajority of the U.S. Senate Democratic Caucus has asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to deploy body cameras to all federal immigration officers, following deadly shootings of immigrants in Texas and Maine.

In a July 19 letter addressed to Mullin, 38 Senate Democrats and Maine’s Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, requested information about the shootings this month in Houston of 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and in Biddeford, Maine, of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.

Neither man was the initial enforcement target when Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers stopped their vehicles, the Department of Homeland Security has said.

“The unnecessary loss of life in these incidents demands immediate, thorough, independent, and transparent investigations (including the full involvement of local and state law enforcement personnel), along with a comprehensive examination of enforcement protocols, training, and operational approaches necessary to prevent such tragedies,” the senators wrote.

The lawmakers pressed Mullin about providing body cameras to immigration officers, pointing out the Congress has allocated $175 billion to the department since last year. From that funding, DHS planned to hire up to 10,000 ICE officers.

“While DHS has previously acknowledged that body-worn cameras promote public trust and increase officer and public safety, accountability, and transparency, the Department has clearly not prioritized acquiring cameras,” the senators wrote.

None of the ICE officers involved in the shootings were wearing body cameras.

“Contrary to recent statements made by the Department and the White House, DHS has had more than sufficient time and funding to procure and deploy a body-worn camera for every officer before the end of 2025,” they wrote.

Enough funding

Congressional Republicans last year used a special legislative maneuver to allocate roughly $175 billion to DHS for immigration enforcement, detainment and deportations, without needing Democratic support.

They used the same move following the shutdown this year to fund $75 billion for ICE and Border Patrol through September of 2029.

Republicans used the maneuver that allows party-line votes after Democrats refused to provide more funding for DHS unless restraints were placed on ICE and Border Patrol officers following the killings of two U.S. citizens — Alex Pretti and Renee Good — by federal immigration agents in Minnesota in January.

Among Democrats’ demands at the time was that immigration officers wear body cameras. Top Trump officials, including then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, said body cameras would be provided to immigration agents.

“The recent tragedies confirm that neither of these commitments were honored,” senators wrote in the letter.

Traffic stops unpaused

White House border czar Tom Homan said over the weekend that ICE officers will wear “at least one body camera” during traffic stops.

Following the two killings this month, DHS instructed immigration officers to pause vehicle stops, but President Donald Trump quickly instructed the department to continue the policy.

During the second Trump administration, federal immigration officers have shot 22 people and killed six, including three U.S. citizens. Most of the shootings stemmed from traffic stops.

In the letter, senators also sought information about DHS’s plan to have an independent investigation into the killings, the vetting process for new immigration officers, the department’s procedures for vehicle stops and any additional oversight and reporting requirements DHS is implementing.

title: Amid ICE killings, churches defend immigrants | UMNews.org
description:
A national crisis Across the U.S., United Methodists are seeking to be the kind of Christ-following neighbors that Chang describes.
More than 50 additional people have died in ICE detention since Trump returned to office.
Helping people in detention United Methodists can help by writing a letter of encouragement to people in detention, Kvalheim said.
The Task Force on United Methodist Immigration Ministries of Ohio has organized a letter campaign for detained asylum seekers.
Among those providing care are members of Morristown and Morrow Memorial United Methodist churches.
text:
A national crisis

Across the U.S., United Methodists are seeking to be the kind of Christ-following neighbors that Chang describes.

With their faith partners, they are holding prayer vigils, comforting the bereaved, supporting families with loved ones in detention and accompanying immigrants through the legal process. They also are calling for an end to government actions that they say terrorize whole communities.

The Rev. Emily Chapman, senior pastor of St. Mark’s United Methodist Church in Houston, is part of the faith-based Migration with Dignity Coalition. The group has been holding prayer vigils at the local detention center and advocating before Houston city leaders to support an independent investigation into Salgado Araujo’s death. Chapman and her ecumenical partners also have advocated for the city to stop cooperating with ICE on non-safety-related traffic stops.

“As it stood, if you got pulled over, the Houston police would wait for ICE for a really long time, even if you were pulled over for your inspection sticker being expired,” Chapman said. “So, it has been pretty horrendous.”

Initially, she said, Houston leaders agreed to limit ICE cooperation, but then the Texas Gov. Greg Abbott threatened to withhold state public safety funds and they reversed course.

Houston, the fourth-largest city in the U.S., has largely seen economic prosperity — not to mention increased food and entertainment options — because of its growing immigrant population, Chapman added.

“Frankly, everything that’s fun and interesting about the city is because of immigrant communities,” she said. “An attack on our immigrant community makes no sense.”

But Chapman and other advocates also are dealing with an increasingly impervious ICE, which received a $75 billion budget boost from the U.S. Congress last year. ICE’s funding now exceeds the budgets of all other federal law enforcement agencies combined. The funds have allowed ICE to expand detention, hire thousands of agents and put them on the streets, often with little training and little restraint on violent tactics. The results have been deadly.

Since Trump retook office in January 2025, at least 10 people have died during federal immigration operations including U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

On July 14, the day after Guerrero’s death, Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran was killed by a truck in St. Augustine, Florida, as he was fleeing ICE agents. The Miami Herald reports that the 28-year-old Mexican man was in Florida on a valid tourist visa and had a flight booked on July 18 to return home.

More than 50 additional people have died in ICE detention since Trump returned to office. The often-overcrowded detention centers are also seeing disease outbreaks with little oversight. Currently, an ICE processing center in Aurora, Colorado, is blocking state health officials from investigating after reports of at least one detainee with tuberculosis.

The data-collection website TRAC found that 70.6% of the more than 65,000 people in ICE detention nationwide as of July 11 had no criminal conviction.

Being in the U.S. without legal documentation is still a civil offense, and not a crime. A ProPublica investigation last year also found ICE has detained more than 170 U.S. citizens since Trump’s second term began.

Yet even as mass deportation efforts mount, Gallup polling shows 73% of Americans think immigration is a good thing for the U.S. Majorities of Americans also oppose deporting all immigrants who are living in the U.S. illegally and would prefer increased pathways to U.S. citizenship.

“As people of conscience and faith, we affirm that every person bears the image of God and possesses inherent dignity, regardless of immigration status,” the United Methodist Immigration Task Force, chaired by retired Bishop Minerva Carcaño, said in a statement.

“No person should lose their life because they were driving to work, providing for their family, or living under the fear created by militarized immigration enforcement.”

Providing legal aid

One of the ways The United Methodist Church seeks to uphold human dignity is through its Immigration Law and Justice Network, which has branches across the U.S. that help immigrants trying to attain legal status and citizenship.

Attorneys at the network’s branches are looking for legal avenues to help Haitians and Syrians who have lost temporary protected status.

“Every now and then, we do have clients who are eligible to obtain their permanent residency through family members or maybe other forms of relief,” said Joy Green, an attorney and executive director of Justice for All Immigrants, the network’s branch in Houston and San Antonio. Her office shares a building with Mission Milby.

People who have lost TPS should reach out to one of the network’s offices or to another immigration attorney, she said.

At the same time, she acknowledged that many in her community are experiencing fear. Immigration cases long have faced bureaucratic hurdles and an overworked court system, but now Green is seeing challenges to legal immigration unlike any she has seen before in her 15-year legal practice.

“A good handful of clients,” she said, have experienced prolonged detention and possible deportation even though they are in the U.S. legally.

“Their family members have reached out and said, ‘Hey, my loved one is detained, and we don’t know why. They have a work permit. They’re authorized to be here. What’s going on?’” she said. “The result is that we have seen an increase in the number of people who we need to help file what we call habeas petitions to try to get them released.”

The Rev. Emily Kvalheim, a United Methodist deacon and immigration attorney in Cleveland, Ohio, said that since January 2025, there have been at least 736 immigration policy changes — most of which have harmed noncitizens no matter their status.

She advises undocumented people to familiarize themselves with their constitutional rights and engage in emergency response planning with their families to prepare for the possibility of detention and deportation.

Helping people in detention

United Methodists can help by writing a letter of encouragement to people in detention, Kvalheim said. The Task Force on United Methodist Immigration Ministries of Ohio has organized a letter campaign for detained asylum seekers.

“You will help to reassure them that they are welcome in our community, their community stands in solidarity with them, and they are not alone during one of the worst times in their lives,” she said.

In the Greater New Jersey Conference, United Methodists have been working with interfaith partners to operate a hospitality tent for families visiting detained loved ones inside the Delaney Hall ICE Detention Facility in Newark. Among those providing care are members of Morristown and Morrow Memorial United Methodist churches.

Their services include providing clothes for family members turned away because of Delaney Hall’s strict dress code. The facility bans visitors from wearing sandals, Crocs, shorts, leggings and any clothes deemed “too provocative.”

Families are forced to wait outside, so volunteers try to provide comfort and welcome in any way they can. Since the fall, a couple from Morristown United Methodist Church has come faithfully every Tuesday to grill hot dogs on a small stove to share with anyone who is hungry. In winter, the couple also passes around hot cocoa.

Volunteers also try to help detainees inside the facility when permitted. One of the apparent goals of Delaney Hall is to get people to self-deport, said the Rev. Danny Yang, senior pastor of Morrow Memorial United Methodist Church. Lights are kept on at all hours. The detention cells are kept either too cold or too hot. And detainees have reported unsanitary conditions including spoiled and sickening food.

Yang, who is fluent in Mandarin, has provided interpretation for a detainee who is trying to return to China but barred from being released to buy her own plane ticket.

“She has to go through the proper channels, and that means that immigration has to work with China to arrange the transportation back,” Yang said. “That’s what she was waiting for, and who knows how long she’ll have to wait? So it’s sad. She had never committed a crime. She was just undocumented. But she was ready to go, and she can’t go, and she’s just stuck there.”

But while the situation is grim, the experience of the hospitality tent has shown people have found all kinds of little ways to help, said the Rev. Luana Cook Scott, Morristown’s senior pastor.

“You can feel like you can’t make a difference in this world right now,” she said. “But when people are waiting to get into the detention center, we can make it less painful and problematic because they have so many other hurdles they are trying to overcome. This is one way we can make a small difference in one person’s life at a time.”

title: Mexico seeks accountability in Chicago-area ICE death and 16 others. Can it force the U.S. to act?
description:
Villegas González had lived in the United States since 2007.
Mexico can’t compel the United States to investigate or collect evidence, experts say.
The consulate did not answer subsequent questions seeking specifics about whether the family has taken legal action into the death of Villegas González.
According to Shaw Drake, an assistant professor at the University of New Mexico School of Law, Mexico could have another source of leverage.
The United States relies heavily on Mexico to accept deportees, including people from countries other than Mexico.
text:
Mexico has begun taking legal action to seek accountability for the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals who have died during U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations — 14 died in ICE custody, and three were killed during other “arrest operations.” This includes Silverio Villegas González, who was shot and killed by an ICE agent during a traffic stop in Franklin Park nearly a year ago.

Villegas González had lived in the United States since 2007. He was the father of two young children.

At the time, the federal Department of Homeland Security said Villegas González had fled a traffic stop and dragged an ICE agent “a significant distance with his car,” seriously injuring the agent. But Franklin Park police body-camera video footage obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times cast doubt on DHS’s description of what happened, catching the ICE agent saying his injuries were “nothing major,” a “knee injury” and “some lacerations” to his hands.

Mexico’s announcement came days after an ICE agent fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston on July 7. The Department of Homeland Security says Salgado Araujo was not the person agents were looking for.

Mexico President Claudia Sheinbaum has referred to these deaths as “homicides.” As she called for more accountability at a news conference announcing steps her government was taking, Sheinbaum said Mexico “cannot turn a blind eye to the Mexicans who have died.

“We are going to do everything within our power,” Sheinbaum said. “What we cannot do is stand by as Mexicans die in ICE operations or detention.”

Mexico’s effort has three tracks. Mexico has filed criminal complaints with state and county prosecutors in Illinois and elsewhere, and it plans to submit a complaint to the U.S. Department of Justice, seeking independent investigations into the deaths. The Mexican government also issued cease- and-desist letters directing U.S. detention centers to preserve records and called for a formal review by the United Nations Human Rights Council.

It will be up to U.S. officials to decide whether to investigate or file charges.

Legal experts and immigration advocates say it’s unclear whether U.S. authorities will cooperate with an investigation but that the process still could put political pressure on the United States to take action and potentially yield evidence that could be used for civil lawsuits.

Can Mexico force the U.S. to investigate?

Mexico can’t compel the United States to investigate or collect evidence, experts say.

Mexico already is encountering resistance from U.S. officials. Earlier this week, Mexico said the State Department returned a cease-and-desist letter it sent regarding four Mexican citizens who died earlier this year at the Adelanto detention center in San Bernardino County.

For any sort of investigation into individual deaths, U.S. prosecutors could determine whether there is a basis to investigate, decline to open an investigation or later decide not to file charges in any of these cases, says Ilan Katz, a Mexico-based criminal defense lawyer who is president of the Mexican Bar Foundation.

“When a government goes to the Department of Justice, it is like any person going to the DOJ,” Katz says. “The department has the discretion to act or not act, but it has now been informed of alleged criminal conduct.”

He says he can’t predict what will happen this time.

“We don’t know, especially because, in the world of Trump, [the] DOJ has become — or at least seems to have become — less independent than it was in the past,” Katz says.

Tom Ginsburg, a University of Chicago law professor who focuses on constitutional and international law, says that, even though the Mexican government can’t force the United States to investigate, it can send an important political message tol Mexican citizens that their government “ is not abandoning them.”

But he says international law can do little to force the United States to take accountability.

“In general, there’s your rights, and then there’s what are the remedies,” he says. “What’s the mechanism for enforcing it?”

He says there are few ways to compel a country to remedy a violation of international law, and the United States has often resisted complying.

“I know no one’s holding their breath with the Trump administration,” he says.

Waiting for answers

Villegas González’s case shows what those limits mean for a family and a community.

Reyna Torres Mendívil, Mexico’s consul general in Chicago, says Mexico first called for an investigation by the FBI on Sept. 13, 2025, a day after Villegas González died. It also sent a diplomatic request to the U.S. Embassy in Mexico.

In a statement, a spokesperson for DHS says the “ criminal prosecution of the involved ICE officer was declined by the United States Attorney’s Office,” but pursuant to ICE policy, “the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility is continuing its administrative review of the incident.“

In May, the Illinois State Police said it had opened an investigation into the death of Villegas González. No results have been made public.

Torres Mendívil said attorneys representing the Villegas family are conducting their own inquiry as they consider possible legal action. “They are carrying out a parallel investigation into the circumstances and everything that happened, for whatever legal action may be appropriate,” Torres Mendívil says.

The consulate did not answer subsequent questions seeking specifics about whether the family has taken legal action into the death of Villegas González.

The consulate cannot represent families directly in U.S. courts, but Torres Mendívil said it can provide money for outside lawyers on a case-by-case basis. “We do provide resources so that attorneys can do it,” she said. “Not in every case. The case has to be viable.”

In Villegas González’s case, she said the consulate is “assisting the family with the payment of the attorneys” working to reunify his children with relatives.

Building a record and pressure

Mexico has also made a formal request to the United Nation to gather information about the deaths, including that of Villegas González, and examine whether the United States met its duties under international law.

The U.N. could ask U.S. officials what happened, review whether the deaths were properly investigated and call for more information, further investigation or changes in U.S. practices.

Sarah Dávila, an associate professor of law at UIC and director of the International Human Rights Clinic who says she was speaking on behalf of herself and not the university, says the United States has a duty under international human-rights law to investigate reports of abuse. But the U.N. Human Rights Council cannot force U.S. agencies to comply.

“While recommendations from the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights are not binding, or findings from United Nations procedures, they carry enormous weight,” Dávila says.

She says those findings could create an independent record and later be used in civil or criminal cases in the U.S.

The cease-and-desist letters do not carry legal force on their own but serve as a formal “warning” not to destroy or alter evidence and can become important if a case later goes to trial, experts say.

Ginsburg says Mexico could also make a case before the U.N. that the rights of its citizens were violated under international law. That could include violations of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, which requires the agency detaining a foreign national to allow the detainee to have access to their consular officials, who could visit them in detention and help them obtain a lawyer.

According to Shaw Drake, an assistant professor at the University of New Mexico School of Law, Mexico could have another source of leverage. The United States relies heavily on Mexico to accept deportees, including people from countries other than Mexico.

“If Mexico refuses to receive those third-country nationals [for deportation], it puts a major wrench in the administration’s current mass deportation efforts,” Drake says.

This could give Mexico’s demands for accountability greater political weight, he said, if the country chooses to use it.

Artemio Arreola, political director of the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights says that even though he thinks Mexico’s announcement is mainly political and diplomatic, investigations are still important because families deserve to know exactly how their relatives died, particularly when evidence has contradicted official accounts.

“These investigations are even more important because, in many of these cases, the official accounts have turned out to be false,” he says.

Senate Bill Follows Successful House Passage of Pressley’s Discharge Petition to Extend TPS for Haitians

Bill Text (PDF) | Letter Text (PDF)

WASHINGTON – Today, ahead of Senate floor action to extend Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Co-Chair of the House Haiti Caucus, alongside Congresswoman Laura Gillen (NY-04), urged Senators to support legislation to extend Haiti TPS and protect the lives and livelihoods of Haitians and Americans alike. Senators Ed Markey and Lisa Blunt Rochester lead the companion bill, introduced after the successful House passage of Congresswoman Pressley’s discharge petition to preserve and extend TPS for Haitians.

In their letter to Senators, the Congresswomen made clear the harm of terminating TPS both for the safety and well-being of Haitian families and for the health of the American economy, workforce, and communities that are beneficiaries of Haitians’ essential contributions.

“Protecting the safety, dignity, and humanity of our Haitian neighbors is the right thing to do, and our country is strengthened by their contributions to our communities, the economy, our healthcare workforce, and more,” said Rep. Pressley. “Since my discharge petition to extend TPS for Haitians successfully passed the House, we’ve been pressing hard to advance this essential legislation and protect our Haitian neighbors. The Senate must pass the extension of Haiti TPS without delay.”

“The Senate must respond to the Supreme Court’s harmful decision to terminate TPS for hardworking, taxpaying, law-abiding Haitian members of our community and pass our bipartisan bill immediately,” said Rep. Gillen. “Haitian TPS recipients have been thoroughly vetted, passed rigorous background checks and are essential to our nation’s workforce. Forcing them to face the violence and chaos in Haiti would be tantamount to a death sentence and bad for our economy. I’m proud to join my colleagues to urge every senator to support our legislation preserving the legal status of our Haitian friends and neighbors.”

The legislation preserves TPS protections for more than 300,000 Haitian nationals, offering a critical lifeline as Haiti continues to confront political instability, widespread violence, and a serious humanitarian emergency.

Bill text can be accessed here.

Congresswoman Pressley serves as Co-Chair for the House Haiti Caucus and represents one of the largest Haitian diaspora communities in the country. She has stood in vigorous defense for Haitian communities and all immigrant neighbors amid Trump and ICE’s attacks against immigrant communities.

text:
North Carolinians should resist efforts to build a new immigrant detention camp in the state — and push back against other policies meant to ramp up deportations — protesters said Wednesday as several dozen gathered outside the state legislature waving signs, singing and delivering speeches.

A month ago, state lawmakers voted to override Democratic Gov. Josh Stein’s veto of a bill requiring many state agencies to cooperate more closely with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, and to take new steps to ensure immigrants aren’t receiving state benefits they’re not eligible for.

Republican President Donald Trump made ramped-up immigration enforcement a key part of his 2016, 2020 and 2024 campaigns. In late 2025 immigration raids across North Carolina saw ICE make hundreds of arrests across the state.

Now, newly public documents have shown the Trump administration is considering opening a detention camp in rural northeastern North Carolina to hold immigrants, after court battles and protests in Florida preceded the closure of a large Everglades camp called “Alligator Alcaraz” by Trump as well as his critics.

One opponent of opening a new immigrant detention camp in North Carolina is Iliana Santillán, the founder of immigrant advocacy group Brava NC. She also serves on a new state Latino Advisory Council that Stein created last year as Trump was ramping up ICE raids.

She said at Wednesday’s protest that the conditions in immigrant detention camps are inhumane — with children separated from their parents, people denied medications, and dozens of deaths recorded in the camps since Trump returned to office last year.

“We have a choice about the North Carolina that we want to be,” Santillán said. “Do we become a place that responds to human suffering with more walls, more detention, and more separation? Or do we choose dignity?”

A White House spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday. In Raleigh, when lawmakers initially voted a year ago to require closer cooperation between state agencies, state law enforcement officials and ICE, a former police chief serving in the legislature said it was the right move.

“There are all commonsense things that need to be done to make sure we are doing what we can, at the state level, to address illegal immigration and protect our citizens," Rep. Reece Pyrtle, R-Rockingham, said at the time, WRAL reported.

On Wednesday a spokesperson for state House Speaker Destin Hall repeated similar arguments in response to the protests.

"It is simply common sense that law-enforcement agencies should work together to identify and remove individuals who are in this country illegally and commit crimes," Hall spokeswomen Demi Dowdy said. "Thanks to these efforts, dangerous offenders are being taken off our streets, and North Carolina communities are safer as a result."

But also joining Hispanic and Latino activists Wednesday were Black, Jewish or Muslim speakers who drew a direct line from slavery and the Holocaust to America’s current policies of immigration raids and detention camps.

“We will not go back to a time of standing by and watching our neighbors be brutalized, captured and trafficked,” said Karen Ziegler of the group Democracy Out Loud. “We will not go back to a time when family separation was the norm and the law. We are called to be the Underground Railroad now, to be the abolitionists now, to be the resistance now.”

Munir Abdul Hakim, the leader of the Triangle-based group Muslims for Social Justice, said his ancestors were enslaved in Franklin County — a family history that leads him to support immigrants who he said now face the threat of violence or mistreatment as they go to work in North Carolina.

“This is not an immigrant issue,” he said. “This is a working class issue, and a human rights issue. Violently grabbing someone off of a job site with no warrant, no hearing is a threat to everyone's freedom.”

New ICE camp in NC?

It doesn’t appear the Stein administration or other state officials would be able to stop a possible new federal detention camp, in Hertford County, from opening even if they wanted.

A state prison system spokesperson told WRAL the facility in question is owned by a private prison company, not the state — and that the state is concerned that a new private prison camp opening up could recruit guards and others away from North Carolina’s already-understaffed state prisons.

Ziegler said it’ll be up to the people to stop it.

“I remember growing up and learning about concentration camps in Germany, and I thought, why don't they just bomb the train tracks?” she said Wednesday. “I don't know what it will take to stop this machine. I believe it is peaceful, massive protest.”

In 2025 the state legislature passed a new law requiring county sheriffs and their deputies to work more closely with ICE agents in North Carolina. And last month the legislature passed another bill into law extending similar rules mandating ICE cooperation by state law enforcement agencies, the state prison system and agencies under Stein’s control.

Berger personally sponsored that newest immigration law — a rare move for a member of leadership — last year as he also sought Trump’s endorsement in his March 2026 primary election. He was successful in winning Trump’s endorsement but came up short in the election, which Berger lost to Rockingham County Sheriff Sam Page by 23 votes.

NC’s new immigration law

The law begins with a lengthy passage praising Trump and criticizing Stein, saying in part that “with their votes electing Donald J. Trump to be the 47th President of our great nation, the American people and the people of North Carolina clearly communicated their strong desire to create a safer country through increased border security and stronger immigration policies.”

Stein said the benefits piece of the bill was unnecessary since state agencies have always had policies in place to ensure that immigrants in the country without legal authorization are blocked from receiving food stamps, Medicaid, Section 8 housing funds and unemployment checks.

And the portions of the bill requiring law enforcement to work more closely with ICE, Stein said, will harm public safety in North Carolina by taking police away from their regular duties.

But GOP lawmakers said Stein hadn’t done enough to help Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda and needed to be forced to have state prison and law enforcement workers do more. They lacked the votes for months to override Stein’s veto, as Democrats in the state House stood behind the governor. Republicans hold a veto-proof supermajority in the state Senate but not the House.

However, after Stein backed a primary challenger this March against Charlotte Rep. Carla Cunningham, and Cunningham lost her race, she quit the Democratic Party in protest.

text:
The Mexican man who was hit and killed by a semi-truck in Florida when running away from federal immigration officials was vacationing in the US with a tourist visa, according to news reports this week.

The 28-year-old, Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, was killed on 14 July after an “encounter” with federal officials, including those with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a state highway patrol spokesperson said last week.

After federal officials approached him and a group of four men at a gas station that Tuesday morning, they all took off running. The Florida highway patrol spokesperson said Coronilla ran into traffic and was hit by a semi-truck.

Coronilla’s death is one of the four ICE-related deaths that took place in less than one week. Two people, one in Texas and one in Maine, were shot and killed by ICE officers. And a fourth person died in ICE custody, while being transferred to an immigration detention center in Georgia. The four deaths have led to renewed calls by the public and lawmakers to reign in ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), as they carry out the Trump administration’s aggressive “mass deportation” campaign promise.

According to the Miami Herald, Coronilla, from the Mexican state of Guanajuato, had only been in Florida for two days when he died, having arrived in the US only three weeks prior. Coronilla had traveled to Atlanta at first to see family and friends and went to Florida to enjoy the beaches.

Coronilla’s wife, who flew to the US last week to make arrangements, had not heard from her husband and found out about his death while watching the news, a local immigrant rights group told the Miami Herald. She then contacted the group, Colectivo Arbol, to ask for help. The group said Coronilla left behind a seven-year-old son and seven-month-old daughter.

DHS has not publicly identified Coronilla, but the Associated Press confirmed his identity with a Mexican government official.

Although the Florida highway patrol’s statement said it was an ICE operation, a homeland security source familiar with the case told the Guardian last week that border patrol agents were involved in the incident.

David Porter is director of engineering with the Department for Infrastructure, which is Northern Ireland’s highways authority. In this role, he is also the chief highways engineer and head of the civil engineering profession in the Northern Ireland civil service.

Porter is responsible for the development of the department’s professional and technical staff, engineering policies and standards, and health and safety. He also leads on procurement and the internal consultancy.

Previously, he was chief executive of the Rivers Agency, Northern Ireland’s flood defence and drainage authority.

Porter has served on the ICE Council three times, twice as the Northern Ireland representative and once as a general member. He is a trustee who, until recently, held the learning society portfolio. He has also served on several institution committees and panels.

A fellow of the Irish Academy of Engineering, Porter was awarded the Poskitt Medal by ICE Northern Ireland in 2017 and the President’s Award by Engineers Ireland in 2018.

Mark Hansford

With a background in both civil engineering and journalism, Mark Hansford has spent more than 25 years as a specialist in disseminating infrastructure knowledge.

After leaving the University of Birmingham with an MEng in 1997, he began his career as an engineer with AtkinsRéalis, where he conducted water supply and distribution analyses, including an asset condition study covering the 100 largest urban water schemes in Ghana.

In 2000, Hansford joined New Civil Engineer magazine, where he progressed through a series of roles. As editor from 2014 to 2020, he led its relaunch as a monthly title publishing daily digital news.

An ICE Fellow, Hansford then served the institution for nearly six years as its director of engineering knowledge. He now works with several organisations seeking to share knowledge, stimulate discussion and enable action to improve the performance of the UK infrastructure sector.

Adrian Johnson

With 30 years of professional experience, Adrian is a chartered civil engineer and executive technical director at Stantec. He’s worked primarily in the water sector, specialising in sustainable development, climate change and carbon management.

Adrian has supported several water company capital programmes and led numerous consultancy and research commissions on topics ranging from carbon accounting, resource efficiency and renewable energy appraisals, to natural capital assessments and climate change risk and resilience. For example, Adrian implemented a carbon and sustainability strategy for Thames Water capital delivery, including priorities for flood resilience and reporting on climate change adaptation. He also provides consultancy support and training for Scottish Water and several of Stantec’s other water clients in the UK and Ireland on their net zero commitments, developing tools and guidance, embedding carbon and other sustainability criteria into decision-making, as well as helping them assess risks from and make plans to adapt to climate change.

Adrian is an Honorary Professor at Heriot-Watt University, School of Energy, Geoscience, Infrastructure and Society. He is also a Fellow of the Institution of Civil Engineers, and Member of the Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management and the UK Green Construction Board’s Infrastructure Working Group. He co-chairs the Technical Advisory Panel (TAP) for PAS 3090 Adaptation Pathways for Infrastructure Systems, and previously chaired the TAP responsible for both the development and subsequent update of PAS 2080 Carbon Management in Buildings and Infrastructure.

Lewis Barlow

Renowned for his work to reduce greenhouse gas emissions on construction projects, Lewis Barlow provides expert advice on whole-life decarbonisation to developers and governments.

With more than 25 years’ experience of managing environmental risk, he is responsible for several internationally recognised advances in tackling the climate crisis.

Barlow and his team won New Civil Engineer’s NCE100 Low Carbon Leader Award two years running for their work to reduce infrastructure assets’ lifetime emissions and share best practice across the sector.

Skilled in applying climate change projections to ensure project resilience, Barlow wrote and presents the ICE’s Carbon Management in Infrastructure course. He was a member of both the steering group and the technical advisory panel for the revised carbon management standard PAS 2080:2023.

Anthony Burd

A chartered building surveyor and engineer, Anthony Burd has more than 36 years’ experience in the sector. He worked for 16 years in government, serving as the UK’s fire regulator and later as head of technical policy for the Building Regulations in England, with energy efficiency and net zero among his responsibilities.

In his current role at the BSI, Burd oversees the creation and promotion of standards for the built environment, working with stakeholders across government and industry to identify new areas for research, standardisation and product development.

He served as president of the Chartered Association of Building Engineers in 2019-20 and was a full member of the statutory Building Regulations Advisory Committee until its abolition in 2023.

text:
HARWICH – Christopher Tansey is a strong believer in Catholic social teachings, a philosophy that emphasizes human dignity, the common good and justice for the most vulnerable.

Tansey, who lives in East Harwich with his wife and son, has a history of exercising that philosophy, especially when it comes to immigrants detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). In 2019, Tansey and Lincoln resident Connor May walked the 140 miles from Dorchester to the Shrine of Divine in Stockbridge to bring attention to the separation of immigrant parents from children when crossing the border from Mexico to the United States.

Tansey and May embarked on another protest walk on Sunday. Starting at the Pilgrim’s First Landing Park in Provincetown, over six days they will conclude their protest pilgrimage outside the Plymouth County Correctional Facility (PCCF) on Friday, July 24.

“Our biggest goal is to raise awareness so the people of Southeastern Massachusetts know what’s going on there,” Tansey said of the treatment of nearly 400 immigrants placed by ICE in the Plymouth County Correctional Facility, where more than 85 percent have not been convicted of a crime.

The pilgrimage is a somewhat familiar journey made by early immigrants in this country. There is symbolism in beginning the walk at the Pilgrims’ First Landing Park in Provincetown and ending it at the Plymouth correctional facility, he said.

“The first immigrants were treated like heroes,” Tansey said, “and people who are now seeking a better life are being incarcerated only two miles from the Plymouth Plantation.”

The pilgrimage will serve to raise funds for detainees with legal expenses and with bond assistance, said Tansey. The money will go to the Boston Immigration Just Accompaniment Network (BIJAN). Tansey and May have set up a GoFundMe account with a goal of raising $5,000. Tansey said as of June 18 they had already raised almost $6,000, so they set a new goal of $10,000.

Their pilgrimage can be followed on Instagram at Plymouthjusticepilgrimage and on Facebook at Plymouth Justice Pilgrimage, which includes a QR code through which donations can be made. They will also be collecting donations during the walk.

Another goal of the pilgrimage is to have people join them as they make their 80-mile journey.

“Walking in solidarity is powerful,” said Tansey. “We see this as a walk for people of all faiths and all political backgrounds. Every human deserves human dignity. Whether you are Republican or a Democrat, you can get on the same page regarding human dignity.”

Ninth Congressional District Democratic Candidate Craig Swallow, who will face off in the September primary against Congressman Bill Keating, D-Bourne, joined the walk. Swallow said he will be walking on five of the six days. A New Bedford resident, Swallow said he got involved in the cause through serving as a co-leader of Indivisible.

Tansey and May met about seven years ago while serving in the Jesuit Volunteer Core at a summer program at the Crow Reservation in Montana. They became roommates while attending graduate school at Boston College. Tansey received a master’s degree in education and May a master’s degree in theology. Tansey is now a middle school teacher in Sandwich and May teaches ethics and social justice at Boston College High School.

The conditions the immigrants suffer at the Plymouth facility are deplorable, according to Tansey, who cited medical deficiencies, poor food quality, meager amounts of food and contaminated products. He said detainees complain of delays in getting medical diagnoses, and ICE refuses to provide diagnostics and specialist consultation.

He cites a 2024 Boston University School of Law’s Immigrants’ Rights and Human Trafficking Program and Prisoners’ Legal Services of Massachusetts report which chronicles 25 years of violations associated with ICE detentions at the Plymouth facility.

“The men we spoke with shared a number of significant concerns including regarding jail conditions, insufficient and/or inedible food, excessively cold temperatures in their cells, lack of access to medical care, lack of language access, inability to communicate with loved ones, and lack of access to legal resources,” according to the report. “They also spoke to a pervasive culture of verbal abuse, racism, intimidation, and retaliation.”

“The food is very bad,” one inmate was quoted as saying in the report. “So, so bad. So many raw potatoes. The rice is hard and inedible. It’s not sufficient calories. Never in six months of being here have I been fed enough calories. Never once in six months have I had eggs or chicken. Just bread, bread and more bread. If we do get meat, it’s like dog food.”

“We are highly concerned that the rights and health of people detained on behalf of ICE at PCCF remain in jeopardy,” Senators Elizabeth Warren and Edward Markey wrote in a letter to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE after a visit in 2022. “Detainees should have access to a safe, dignified, and lawful environment. ICE officials and contractors must be transparent about how they treat people in their custody, and held accountable if they have refused to treat people in their custody consistent with basic human dignity and DHS rules and regulations.”

Tansey said Senator Markey made a return visit to the Plymouth facility a couple of months ago and called conditions he saw there “deeply concerning” in a YouTube presentation.

Solitary confinement is used not as a punishment but is based on administrative decisions, he said.

There has been a sharp uptick in phone calls regarding medical care at the facility in the past few months, according to a statement issued by Leah Hastings, a lawyer with Prisoners’ Legal Services of Massachusetts. Tansey said ICE has not been processing outside claims for medical services since last October, citing insufficient funds. Detainees suffer for weeks with tooth infections, he said.

ICE provides $10 million a year to PCCF, and the facility receives $200 per person per day. PCCF is the only county correctional facility in the state with a contract with ICE, according to Tansey.

On Sunday, Tansey and May departed Provincetown and walked to South Wellfleet along Route 6. On Monday, they walked mainly on the Cape Cod Rail Trail, ending in Orleans. Tansey said on Sunday that about 10 people joined them on the walk from Provincetown and 10 to 15 people accompanied them on Monday as they took to the rail trail in South Wellfleet.

On Tuesday, they were scheduled to start at Freeman’s Way and move through Brewster, ending at the Ice Cream Smuggler in South Dennis. On Wednesday, they will pass through West Barnstable and end at First Church UCC in Sandwich. On Thursday, they plan to make it over the bridge and end the day outside the YMCA in Plymouth, and on Friday, they will start at Plymouth South High School and end in the area of the Plymouth correctional facility.

text:
The aftermath of last summer’s militarized mass deportation campaign still reverberates in many of L.A. County’s Latino business corridors, this according to a UCLA report published on Wednesday.

The report, rooted in quantitative data and conversations with entrepreneurs countywide, was conducted by UCLA’s nonpartisan Latino Policy and Politics Institute and Inclusive Action for the City, a nonprofit based in Boyle Heights.

The participants include people who run restaurants, bakeries, hair salons, childcare centers, auto repair shops, furniture stores and other brick-and-mortar businesses. Most are located in neighborhoods that were most targeted by federal immigration agents.

In the summer of 2025, L.A. County became the focal point of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. Federal immigration agents carried out operations at commercial corridors that serve as important economic hubs for Latino communities, as well as in residential areas and public spaces. Amid roving patrols and large-scale raids, the federal government deployed thousands of National Guard troops and hundreds of Marines to support these efforts, further militarizing the region.

The institute's report found that, since then, many entrepreneurs are still struggling to keep their businesses open. Some have taken on debt and made other sacrifices to stay afloat.

Amada Armenta, one of the lead researchers and director of the UCLA Latino Policy and Politics Institute, underscored that the consequences of the raids go beyond economics.

In April, she and her colleagues conducted a series of focus groups for the report. And, “without fail,” Armenta added, at least one participant would end up in tears.

The entrepreneurs cried about the effects the raids had on their businesses, she said. They also cried about the toll they took on their health and on their families.

How the researchers calculated economic loss

First, the researchers identified nine places that were subject to enforcement actions, with the goal of sampling a wide breadth of neighborhoods across L.A. County. Ultimately, they landed on businesses in:

Cypress Park

the Fashion District

Huntington Park

Pacoima

Paramount

Whittier

Ladera Heights

the Warehouse District

Westlake

The researchers identified 989 businesses within that half a mile by measuring cellphone data near raids.

After that, “we looked to see how many cell phones visited those businesses in the two weeks after a raid happened, compared to the two weeks before,” Armenta told LAist.

That’s how the researchers determined that, after last summer’s raids, the businesses had 46,000 fewer visits. Then, the researchers estimated the lost revenue. In the two weeks after the raids, they calculated a loss of $3.16 million.

The price of chronic fear and distress

To learn more about how businesses in those areas have fared since last summer, the research team conducted surveys and focus groups with 75 entrepreneurs.

The participants, Armenta said, shared “stories of tremendous hardship,” describing chronic fear and psychological distress.

In the surveys, the entrepreneurs repeatedly described a sustained sense of fear, anxiety, depression and hypervigilance. The entrepreneurs continue to limit their movement outside work and home; carry identification documents when they leave the house; monitor community reports of federal agent activity; and develop contingency plans for themselves, their families and their employees.

For many, dreams of expansion are gone. The entrepreneurs described having to lay off some of their employees, taking on more hours themselves and consolidating locales.

The stress of mounting bills has also taken a physical toll on the participants. One store owner described relapsing into alcohol use after maintaining sobriety. She attributed the relapse to prolonged feelings of helplessness and loss of control. Another business owner said the stress of seeing her family’s savings dry up caused her so much stress her face became paralyzed.

“We thought this was an important part of the story,” Armenta said. “There's been a couple of other reports that have come out about the way that the raids impact L.A.'s economy or businesses, but none of it has documented [their] effect on entrepreneurs.”

“And when we think about Latinos, particularly, they didn't just experience this as an attack on their businesses,” she added. “They experienced it as an attack on their communities, on their families, on themselves.”

text:
EL PASO, Texas (KTSM) — For weeks, Jorge Luis Vilchez opened his restaurant to organizers collecting donations to send to his native Venezuela in the wake of the devastating earthquakes that rocked the country in June.

Vilchez told KTSM 9 News days after the relief efforts began, he was doing his best to help provide a space for El Pasoans to bring goods, but also get to know a little more about Venezuelan culture and the people.

“By doing our part here, lending the restaurant as a collection center, I think we’re contributing so that everyone here in the El Paso community can do their part, both our fellow Venezuelans and Mexicans, Colombians – everyone here in El Paso has come and done their part,” he said.

Vilchez has lived in the United States since 2019; he moved around looking for work until he called El Paso home. According to a family GoFundMe, he’s also waiting on a decision on his asylum case.

But last week, ICE agents detained Vilchez.

“On July 16, ICE arrested Jorge Luis Vilchez Lopez, an illegal alien from Venezuela. He entered the U.S. on September 22, 2019, on a visa and overstayed the visa, which expired on March 21, 2020. All of his claims will be heard by a Justice Department immigration judge, and he will receive full due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” a Department of Homeland Security Spokesman said.

His family says Vilchez has worked hard, respected the law and contributed positively to his community in response to his detainment.

text:
The Trump administration faces an arduous legal path and due process questions as it activates a never-before-used court for suspected noncitizen terrorists.

The Justice Department’s National Security Division launched the case last week in the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, or ATRC, and is set to further detail its application in a sealed brief Wednesday. It’s the first case to go before the court since its creation in 1996.

Congress created the ATRC to handle individual deportation hearings involving suspected terrorists based on highly sensitive information that would threaten national security if released.

Past administrations have avoided mobilizing the court, in part due the availability of other legal avenues for a suspected terrorist’s detainment and continued supervision, said former national security officials at DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security. Other obstacles are the court’s strict standard for using classified information and concerns that individuals can be deported without viewing the government’s evidence against them.

“This is essentially stepping into a car that has never run since it was released from the factory legislatively,” said Aram Gavoor, senior counsel for national security at DOJ during Trump’s first term and the start of Joe Biden’s administration.

“Because it’s a series of firsts, naturally the court is going to want to get it right,” Gavoor said.

Judges on the long dormant court are likely to closely examine DOJ’s arguments as the administration faces broad scrutiny from the federal judiciary over due process concerns from detained immigrants and other challenges to President Donald Trump’s deportation agenda, the former officials said.

DOJ spokesperson Emily Covington said the department plans to “use every tool available to bring alien terrorists to justice and remove them from the United States, including this court.”

Covington didn’t comment further on the case, which remains under seal with details classified.

Dormant History

The administration’s activation of the court surprised former DOJ and DHS lawyers who said the federal government has long pursued alternative counterterrorism and deportation avenues.

At the time of its creation, the ATRC was seen as a top legislative counterterrorism priority. It was modeled after the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, which reviews and approves federal government applications for electronic surveillance and other actions related to national security investigations.

The ATRC is made up of five US district court judges appointed by the chief justice of the United States. All current members also serve on the intelligence surveillance court.

Under federal law, the ATRC may grant a removal application if the government shows that the identified individual qualifies under the definition of an “alien terrorist” and that removal through another legal avenue would pose national security risks.

A 2004 report from a bipartisan national commission on terrorism found DOJ attorneys had reviewed at least 100 cases for possible applications since the court’s creation, but all were rejected.

During the Obama administration, DOJ’s National Security Division examined the ATRC when reviewing authorities available to remove Al-Qaeda in Iraq members living in the US, where establishing their connections to terrorism relied on classified information, said Chris Hardee, who served as the division’s chief of law and policy from 2013 until last year.

“We concluded that it would not help in any case because, even if we could not pursue terrorism charges, there were criminal and immigration options that avoided relying on classified information, such as immigration fraud,” Hardee said.

Those were “far preferable” options than relying on “a novel law in a specialized court that had never heard a case,” he added.

The ATRC’s mission also conflicts with the “entire philosophy of counterterrorism,” said Thomas Warrick, a former longtime DHS counterterrorism official.

“If we had evidence that somebody was a terrorist, and especially if they’d committed terrorist acts against the United States, the whole purpose was to try to bring them here so they could be prosecuted, convicted, and then put in jail,” said Warrick, now at the Atlantic Council.

Once someone leaves the US, “you lose oversight over what they’re doing or who their contacts are,” he said.

Logistical Hurdles

Numerous obstacles, including requirements in the statute for using classified information, await the Trump administration as it moves ahead with its application, immigration policy analysts said.

By law, the government can only admit classified evidence when the ATRC determines the government’s unclassified summary of the case is “sufficient to enable the alien to prepare a defense.”

If an ATRC judge deems the proposed unclassified summary inadequate, the judge may approve the application and move to a hearing under two conditions. The judge must find that both the individual’s continued presence in the US and the provision of a case summary would cause serious and irreparable harm to national security or a person’s physical safety.

Lawful permanent residents must be appointed a special attorney to review and challenge any classified evidence on the resident’s behalf.

That leaves concerns on whether noncitizens who don’t hold this legal status could be deported without the opportunity to review DOJ’s secretive evidence, said Margy O’Herron, a Biden-era senior immigration adviser who served nearly two decades as a DOJ attorney.

As the Trump administration has attempted to use other scarcely invoked laws to advance its deportation agenda, including the 1798 Alien Enemies Act, the activation of the ATRC “appears to be the latest weapon in its scorched-earth deportation strategy,” O’Herron said.

The secretive nature of the court also limits the ability of the public and Congress to hold DOJ accountable, said Elora Mukherjee, director of Columbia Law School’s Immigrants’ Rights Clinic.

The only insight into the court’s perspective thus far came in a July 16 order for DOJ’s supplemental briefing. ATRC Chief Judge Joan Ericksen wrote that the court had questions “about the nexus that the government alleges between the actions of the respondent and the specific sections and subsections it invokes with respect to those actions.”

“The answers persuaded the Court that the Government could benefit from the opportunity for more thoughtful consideration,” Ericksen said.
